item.title: Kerkoporta: Injecting Structured-Output Backdoors in Reasoning Coding Agents
item.description: arXiv:2611.00138v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing large language model (LLM) backdoor attacks operate primarily in chat settings, where the risk is bounded by free-form text outputs. AI agents remove that bound by performing actions and executing commands on the user's machine. We introduce structured-output backdoor attacks against reasoning models in agentic coding settings. A trigger placed anywhere in the agent's context causes the model to emit an attacker-chosen tool call, which the harness executes, directly compromising the system's confidentiality, integrity, or availability. We present Kerkoporta, a methodology that constructs high-quality poison samples, injects the backdoor via supervised fine-tuning, and recovers utility loss with lightweight reinforcement learning. We evaluate on modern, heavily post-trained open-weight models across proprietary and open-source harnesses, focusing on coding for its wide adoption and long-horizon task structure. The attack reaches success rates of up to 96.2% and can be configured to generalize across harnesses or bind to a single target. The resulting models can outperform the clean baseline on standard utility benchmarks, giving victims a direct incentive to adopt them. Overall, we demonstrate that LLM backdoors can have critical security impacts in the context of modern coding agents, and we characterize the poisoning methodology required to insert backdoors that are both effective and stealthy in this setting.
item.dc:creator: Georgios Syros, Blake Bullwinkel, Alina Oprea, Cristina Nita-Rotaru, Amanda Minnich, Xiaodong Liu, Giorgio Severi

item.title: When appearance and motion disagree: evaluating class--motion consistency against disguised uncrewed surface vessels
item.description: arXiv:2611.00367v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Defense systems for maritime assets must distinguish approaching benign craft from uncrewed surface vessels (USVs) with sufficient warning to act. Shore cameras using computer vision can separate hostile vessels from benign traffic, but these systems may be attacked using an adversarial hull patch or physical disguise. We evaluate adversarial hull patches and find they suppress detection in up to 29% of attempts but never cause misclassification as benign. Physical disguise, however, can bypass both a camera check and a radar presence check. To evaluate defenses, we develop a hybrid replay protocol from automatic identification system (AIS) tracks that combines recorded benign motion with direct or off-axis attack run-ins. We find that for recreational-labeled vessels attacking via direct run-in within 4 nautical miles, an asset-relative closing-rate check flags 94-95% at 15-20 knots, compared with 12% for a track-only speed check. The checks are complementary on off-axis approaches, constraining the attacker to remain below both thresholds and extending the time required to reach the asset. Flagging on either check has a 4.9% held-out false-alarm rate overall and 12.3% on recreational traffic. The replay-based evaluation protocol supports comparative test and evaluation of defense methods.
item.dc:creator: Jon Reifschneider

item.title: Threat Modeling Intimate Partner Abuse in Agentic Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.00489v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic systems are AI-powered technologies capable of autonomous action within digital environments, such as sending emails or making reservations. They are deeply connected to external tools as well as users' data and resources, making them vulnerable to attacks which exploit their access and capabilities. In this work, we apply the technology-facilitated abuse threat model, in the context of intimate partner violence and surveillance, to these systems, revealing threats that require deliberate investigation and mitigation. We categorize attacks based on system ownership: (1) Abuser-as-owner attacks demonstrate how agentic systems make existing forms of technology-facilitated abuse far easier and more scalable. (2) Victim-survivor-as-owner attacks show how agentic systems create a new attack surface which abusers can exploit. In light of these risks, we outline research and development directions for effective mitigation strategies.
item.dc:creator: Natalie Grace Brigham, Eugene Bagdasarian, Franziska Roesner, Tadayoshi Kohno

item.title: Practical Preimages for 19- and 20-Step SHA-256 with Standard Padding
item.description: arXiv:2611.00512v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present practical preimage attacks on 19- and 20-step SHA-256 that respect the standard IV, Davies-Meyer feed-forward, and full FIPS 180-4 padding, for arbitrary prescribed 256-bit targets. Building on Basra's algebraic selector saturation and backward padding absorption, we introduce three techniques: an exact $O(1)$ inversion of the low padding byte $(W_{13} \bmod 256) = \mathtt{0x80}$ that leaves $(a_5, a_6)$ free for exact context shaping; a causal bit-slice equivalence theorem that prunes $99.74\%$ of right-hand candidate nodes across seven stages; and a closed-form $\mathbf{F}_2$ upper-half inverse paired with compact $Q_0^{-1}$ lookup tables. One CPU core solves arbitrary 19-step padded targets in $1.2$--$86.4$ s (median $19.5$ s) after an $18$ s table build. A 20-step padded preimage costs $2^{46.6}$ CPU-reference evaluations: $191$ node-hours on one 10-core Apple M4 CPU node (16 threads), or $9.0$--$22.2$ GPU-hours on one NVIDIA L4. A companion Zero-$a_3$ bridge inverts the unpadded 20-step compression function in $2^{38.1}$ evaluations. We provide 46 self-verifying witnesses, including 55-byte preimages of SHA-256("abc") and $0^{256}$. These attacks cover 19--20 of 64 steps and do not threaten full SHA-256.
item.dc:creator: Sebastian R. Wain

item.title: Price is Only the Symptom: Understanding and Analyzing Economic-State Manipulation Vulnerabilities in DeFi
item.description: arXiv:2611.00587v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Economic-state manipulation has emerged as a significant security threat to decentralized finance (DeFi), causing substantial financial losses. Existing studies predominantly characterize these attacks as price manipulation, focusing on observable price distortions while overlooking underlying violations of economic-state integrity. We conduct a comprehensive empirical study of Economic-State Manipulation (ESM) vulnerabilities in DeFi. We first curate a diverse dataset comprising 276 real-world attacks and 91 Code4rena audit findings. Based on these cases, we develop a cause-oriented taxonomy comprising four primary categories and eleven subcategories. Our analysis reveals that ESM vulnerabilities extend beyond conventional price manipulation, frequently involving violations of protocol-internal accounting, AMM state consistency, and execution-time constraints. We further investigate the evaluation datasets of six existing studies and find that, although they cover 6-10 vulnerability subcategories, their distributions remain dominated by limited manipulation mechanisms. Furthermore, we systematically evaluate seven representative detection approaches on our dataset. Our results reveal limited coverage, with the best-performing approach identifying only 50.4% of real-world attacks. Through an analysis of false negatives and false positives, we identify fundamental limitations arising from reliance on predefined attack patterns, insufficient reasoning about economic-state semantics, and incomplete exploitability validation. These findings provide empirical insights for developing more generalizable ESM vulnerability detection techniques.
item.dc:creator: Hao Wu, Haijun Wang, Xiapu Luo, Ming Fan, Ting Liu

item.title: Beyond Sensitive APIs: Detecting Access Control Flaws at Sensitive Callsites in Android Firmware
item.description: arXiv:2611.00594v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing studies of vulnerable pre-installed Android apps identify dangerous behavior by checking whether an app invokes an API from a predefined set of security-sensitive APIs. These sets usually exclude generic APIs to avoid false positives; unfortunately, this misses a class of vulnerabilities in which a generic API, such as a database read, appears benign in general but becomes security-sensitive when operating on protected data, yet is left without sufficient access control. While this class of vulnerabilities appears addressable via access control analysis, existing studies focus only on the presence of checks, not on whether those checks enforce sufficient protection for the operation at a given callsite. In this work, we propose Callix, which first assesses callsite sensitivity by jointly analyzing the invoked API functionality and the data involved in the operation, then recovers each security check on the execution path as an explicit security property, and finally introduces the notion of restriction context to decide whether these checks are sufficient for the identified sensitive operation. We evaluated Callix on 1,750 distinct pre-installed apps from the 10 top-tier Android vendors as of 2025. In total, Callix discovered 819 vulnerable paths across these vendors, 42.1% of which allow reading or modifying private user data through generic database operations. Manual validation of a random 60% sample shows a precision of 95.1%. Many of our findings have been confirmed and rewarded through vendor bug bounty programs.
item.dc:creator: Haotian Deng, Meng Hao, Hanxiao Chen, Xinyuan Qian, Guowen Xu, Hongwei Li, Chaoshun Zuo

item.title: Adversarial Robustness Is Not Zero-Day Generalization: A Controlled Evaluation of Flow-Based Intrusion Detectors on Corrected CIC-IDS2017
item.description: arXiv:2611.00713v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Synthetic variants of known attacks, including feature-space adversarial perturbations, are sometimes used as stand-ins for unseen ("zero-day") attacks when evaluating machine-learning network intrusion detection systems (NIDS). We test whether this proxy holds. On the corrected CIC-IDS2017 release we train Random Forest, XGBoost, a 1D-CNN and an FT-Transformer and compare, at a fixed 1% false-positive rate over five seeds, detection under constrained perturbations of known attacks (gradient-based and black-box attacks on 42 attacker-controllable features) with leave-one-attack-family-out (LOAO) detection, where an entire family is absent from training. Detection under the strongest perturbation we tested, with budgets of at most 0.2, stays between 90.9% and 99.7%, yet mean detection of held-out families falls to 76.2% (RF), 40.2% (XGBoost), 25.8% (1D-CNN) and 22.8% (FT-Transformer). Robustness exceeds LOAO detection for every model (gaps of 24 to 72 percentage points, 23 to 66 when robustness is also averaged over families; Holm-adjusted p $\le$ 0.00096), and the two measures agree at most on a coarse ranking of the models. An exact mixed-integer evasion search confirms the tree ensembles' scores. Benign-only anomaly detectors and a simple multi-class open-set baseline do not close the gap. A temporal split on 5 seeds (3 of the 4 models) leaves the gap in place. On CSE-CIC-IDS2018 the gap recurs for every model (16 to 68 points). On these benchmarks and under this threat model, a robustness score should not be read as a zero-day score, and the two should be reported separately. Code and per-seed results are publicly available.
item.dc:creator: Abdulhamid Zaro

item.title: The Long Con on the Web: Earn-then-Exploit Fraud Attacks against Coding Agents
item.description: arXiv:2611.00725v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agents increasingly operate with web access and high privileges, creating a new attack surface where web fraud can directly target autonomous agents. Existing studies mainly focus on malicious links, prompt injection, and interface deception, while content-level web fraud against agents and the amplification of attacks through agent trust remain underexplored. In this paper, we present EtE (Earn-then-Exploit), a web fraud attack framework against coding agents, in which a malicious website first provides multiple rounds of genuinely verifiable assistance to establish trust and then introduces task-related instructions that cross intended operational boundaries. To systematically evaluate its effectiveness, we construct 56 organizational environments (8 task contexts x 7 attack consequences) and evaluate three representative coding agents. EtE achieves an average scene-level attack success rate of 71.4%, including 85.7% on Codex-GPT-5.5, 67.9% on ZCode-GLM-5.3-Flash, and 60.7% on QwenCode-Qwen3.7-Plus, significantly outperforming all injection-based baselines. More importantly, our experiments reveal that coding agents exhibit trust-like behavioral reliance on previously helpful Web sources, and that such accumulated credibility significantly increases their susceptibility to subsequent malicious instructions. Based on this finding, we propose action-authorization separation (AAS), which prevents web content from directly authorizing privileged actions and reduces the attack success rate to 0% while preserving 100% task completion, outperforming all evaluated defense baselines.
item.dc:creator: Xingling Xu, Zhengwei Jiang, Zheng Zhi, Fangming Dong, LingJia Guo, Wei Dong, Chunyan Ma, Jun Jiang

item.title: AgentCap: Capability-Based Runtime Authorization for Secure LLM Agent Execution
item.description: arXiv:2611.00729v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language-model agents commonly collapse two decisions that security systems separate: selecting an action and determining whether that action is authorized. When a model exercises standing authority, indirect prompt injection can convert influence over its reasoning into unauthorized effects. We present AgentCap, a runtime authorization layer that externalizes this decision from the model and mediates every tool invocation through an MCP wrapper. Each request declares an intent, and AgentCap evaluates policy constraints over trust, workflow prerequisites, mutually exclusive authority, and the provenance of security-sensitive arguments. Authorized requests receive short-lived, budget-bounded capability tokens that are validated at the tool boundary. Delegation is restricted to session-bound parent-child chains that preserve action and resource while budget and lifetime can only be attenuated, preventing authority from being expanded or reused across unrelated agent sessions. A declarative policy language provides a common representation for runtime enforcement and predeployment analysis. Across AgentDojo and InjecAgent, AgentCap reduces attack success in every evaluated model-benchmark setting, including zero attack success with GPT-5.4 on both benchmarks. Controlled adversarial scenarios further show that AgentCap blocks every attempted unauthorized execution (ASR 0%) while preserving all legitimate operations exercised. These results demonstrate that agent security requires authorization of model-proposed effects at the tool boundary, independently of the model's reasoning.
item.dc:creator: Aravinda Kashyap Kabbinamakki Suresh, Peng Gao

item.title: Cross-Evidence Authorization State Learning for Runtime Detection of Broken Object-Level Authorization in Black-Box Web Applications
item.description: arXiv:2611.00738v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Broken object-level authorization (BOLA) remains difficult to detect in black-box Web applications because external runtime monitors generally lack access to source code, authorization policies, and object-ownership records. This paper proposes a cross-evidence authorization-state learning method that reconstructs subject--resource--object--action relations from request--response transactions. The method represents authorization relations with confidence-aware states, aggregates positive and negative evidence while accounting for provenance independence, and applies contamination-gated promotion, evidence quarantine and rollback, expiration, and revocation. A Python prototype is evaluated using a deterministic synthetic benchmark comprising 64,400 requests across five independent random seeds. In this benchmark, the proposed method achieves 100.00% recall, an F1-score of 56.63%, and a false-positive rate of 33.65%, while the measured unauthorized-relation pollution rate is 0.00%. Ablation experiments show that removing provenance independence or evidence quarantine increases the pollution rate to 100.00%. The experiments provide an initial evaluation under controlled synthetic conditions.
item.dc:creator: Siqi Lin, Qianheng Cheng, Yiping Mao

item.title: Intent-Bound Authorization for Cryptocurrency Withdrawals Under Backend Compromise
item.description: arXiv:2611.00839v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Binance's preliminary account of its October 2026 attack raises a custody question that key protection alone cannot answer: how can a provider prevent unauthorized withdrawals when an attacker controls a service permitted to request signatures? We propose the Intent-Bound Withdrawal Authorization Protocol (IWAP). Before signing, independent enforcement checks customer intent, exact transaction effects, fresh workload evidence, and a committed single-use spending reservation. Administrative actions use a separate authorization path. We specify the protocol's trust assumptions and give conditional arguments for intent preservation, replay resistance, and a fixed-epoch exposure bound. A Python reference monitor authenticates synthetic records with Ed25519 and serializes reservations with SQLite. It rejects 1,200 negative requests, accepts 3,000 valid synthetic requests, and preserves a 100-unit budget under 64 concurrent attempts in each of 20 trials. When the intent authority is deliberately compromised, malicious requests pass, but the independent budget still limits admitted exposure. The study evaluates a normalized policy model, not Binance's infrastructure or a deployed custody platform. Its contribution is an explicit authorization boundary and reproducible tests of that boundary.
item.dc:creator: Toqeer Ali Syed, Asadullah Abdullah Khan, Ali Akrama

item.title: Illusion: Safeguarding Topology Confidentiality in LLM Multi-Agent Systems via Behavior-Preserving Obfuscation
item.description: arXiv:2611.00923v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The communication topology of Large Language Model Multi-Agent Systems (LLM-MASs) governs how information propagates among agents and encodes critical domain knowledge and expert workflow design. It is valuable intellectual property and plays a decisive role in system utility and safety, yet remains vulnerable to inference attacks that stealthily reconstruct it from agent outputs. Existing defenses detect or mitigate such attacks but do not proactively conceal the topology itself. We propose \textit{Illusion}, a proactive topology obfuscation defense for LLM-MAS. \textit{Illusion} injects fake edges and fake messages to present attackers with a deceptive topology, while selecting low-impact candidates that preserve output-distribution equivalence and task-accuracy non-inferiority. The resulting fake edges are designed to be indistinguishable from genuine messages under black-box observation. Extensive experiments show that \textit{Illusion} reduces edge-level F1 from over 0.87 to 0.62 and graph similarity from over 0.94 to 0.71. It also largely preserves output distributions and task performance, and its fake edges resist both similarity-based and LLM-judge filtering, even under adaptive pruning.
item.dc:creator: Yiu-Fai Cheung, Hongzhi Guo, Miao Pan, Irwin King, Hao Wang

item.title: E-UDE: A Scientific Machine Learning Model for Malware Propagation Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.00971v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding the malware propagation dynamics over the Internet is crucial for effectively controlling its spread. Existing mechanistic and data-driven models in the context of malware propagation dynamics, have some issues with either interpretability or predictive accuracy. This study presents an Enhanced Universal Differential Equation (E-UDE) framework that explicitly incorporates more detailed key factors that influence malware propagation. Evaluation on real-world malware propagation data shows that the E-UDE achieves the best overall performance, attaining an overall RMSE of 783.70 and MAE of 421.65. Compared with the Classical ODE and the UDE models, the proposed approach reduces RMSE by approximately 66 percent and 39 percent, respectively. Its robustness to predictive capability is further evaluated. In this experiment, the E-UDE achieves a Test RMSE of 634.6, a Test MAE of 419.3, and a Test Correlation of 0.964. The E-UDE maintains relatively stable prediction performance as the noise level increases, showing limited degradation compared with the baseline models. Furthermore, this E-UDE model enables us to perform several scenario analyses under different cybersecurity scenarios, providing a useful framework for better understanding the effective control factors. To study the wide applicability of the E-UDE framework, the model performance is assessed by two different datasets, namely, Code Red dataset and Witty Worm dataset.
item.dc:creator: Vineet Kumar, Samiran Ghosh, V Anil Kumar

item.title: Trouble With Time: Compile Timestamps and First-Seen Date Regression in EMBER2024
item.description: arXiv:2611.01031v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reliable first-seen dates are important for constructing temporal malware evaluation splits, but this information often comes from external services that are not equally accessible to all researchers. We investigate whether machine learning can instead estimate an executable's first-seen date or determine when its PE/COFF compilation timestamp is unreliable. Using EMBER2024, we evaluate feature-based and raw-byte models across classification, regression, ranking, and latent-reliability formulations. Direct first-seen regression produces errors comparable to a substantial portion of the dataset's collection window, and none of the evaluated scores provides a useful chronological ordering of files. Current models therefore cannot replace externally sourced first-seen metadata. In contrast, classifiers can identify timestamps that fall within specified tolerances of first seen and can detect clearly implausible timestamps with high discrimination. We also find substantial timestamp disagreement among both benign and malicious executables, indicating that unreliable timestamps are not exclusively a product of malicious manipulation. These results establish baselines and identify timestamp reliability as a distinct direction for future security-ML research.
item.dc:creator: Edward Raff, Aditya Kapoor

item.title: VeilFL: Two-Stage Accountability for Anonymous Federated Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.01082v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Anonymous credentials can hide which registered client participates in federated learning, but their unlinkability also makes repeated misconduct difficult to associate. We present VeilFL, a two-aggregator protocol that adds staged accountability to PINE (USENIX Security '24). Each submission binds two private PINE messages, a round-specific pseudonym, and a tracing pair to the same hidden credential secret. This design enables detection of duplicate submissions within a round without introducing a persistent identifier for normal participation. VeilFL implements accountability in two stages. After a confirmed duplicate or joint PINE rejection, a threshold tracing committee reveals a stable handle that links faults associated with the same credential. The client's registered identity is recoverable only after the public log records the requisite number of linked faults and a separate threshold committee authorizes identification. Accepted and unopened submissions remain unlinkable under the stated assumptions. This work establishes submission binding and duplicate detection, anonymity, fault non-frameability, controlled two-stage opening, and preservation of PINE's privacy and validity guarantees. In the prototype implementation, creating a submission requires a median of 2.11 ms, while verification requires 3.01 ms. Batch verification reduces the cost to 1.86 ms per submission for a batch of 1,000. The public part of each submission is 608 bytes, with 1,248 bytes of additional VeilFL protocol data across the two aggregator submissions. Each opening stage completes within 4.3 ms for the different committee configurations.
item.dc:creator: Varesh Mishra, Aysajan Abidin, Bart Preneel

item.title: Pop Goes the Verifier: Phoneme-Targeted Data Poisoning of Voice Liveness Detection
item.description: arXiv:2611.01095v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many Automated Speaker Verification Systems (ASVs) commonly employ liveliness detection techniques, such as VoicePop, which identify genuine speech by analyzing low- frequency pop bursts from plosive phonemes using Gammatone Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (GFCC) and an SVM classifier. While effective against traditional replay attacks, such systems are vulnerable to data poisoning techniques. Prior work shows that broadly applied SyntheticPop attacks can collapse model to accuracy to as low as 14.01% using only 20% poisoned samples, but the resulting artifacts are easily detectable when visualizing the waveform energies. This paper introduces Pop Goes the Verifier, a stealthier phoneme injection poisoning attack. By leveraging FastSpeech 2 (FS2) with a modified HiFi-GAN vocoder, we inject localized pop bursts at plosive phoneme locations and overlay subtle Gaussian noise to reduce the visibility of injected artifacts in waveform and spectrogram analysis. Using the ASVSpoof 2019 as the dataset, we observe that the approach achieves a moderate poisoning attack while providing greater resistance to signal-level inspection than the original SyntheticPop attack.
item.dc:creator: Eshaq Jamdar, Amith Kamath Belman

item.title: The Blind Spots of Detection: Adversarial Perturbation Attacks against Watchdogs in Distributed LLM Inference
item.description: arXiv:2611.01097v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decentralizing large language model (LLM) inference across untrusted Web nodes requires robust verification to ensure computational integrity. Existing activation-based verification and detection mechanisms validate intermediate outputs against reference values, permitting bounded numerical deviations to accommodate benign cross-hardware discrepancies. However, a critical security question remains: what can a malicious worker achieve while operating within these tolerance bounds? In this work, we introduce Hush-Up, a stealthy availability attack against distributed LLM inference, where a single malicious worker halts generation while evading attribution. The attacker first profiles its local execution to model an empirical bound of benign hardware errors. Using this error bound as a feasibility constraint, the attacker optimizes an adversarial perturbation on its output activations to maximize the final-layer probability of the end-of-sequence (EOS) token, i.e., to hush up the model. Across diverse models and benchmarks, Hush-Up effectively forces premature generation termination and collapses model capabilities. Furthermore, the attack hushes up the watchdogs themselves: existing defenses often fail to detect the sabotage entirely or falsely attribute the amplified downstream anomalies to honest workers. Our findings expose a fundamental gap between local numerical verification and end-to-end accountability: perturbations too small to indict a worker locally can nevertheless be powerful enough to break distributed inference globally.
item.dc:creator: Siu Wai Shi, Xiaochen Zhu, Xinjian Luo, Keke Huang, Bingxue Zhang, Xiaofeng Gao

item.title: What Must Be Done Here? Using a Bounded Application-Security Ontology at the Point of Change
item.description: arXiv:2611.01127v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The security guidance that bears on code is real but scattered. It lives across secure-development frameworks, verification standards, controls catalogues, threat taxonomies, and, increasingly, normative regimes such as the EU's NIS2 -- and most of it is written for readers other than the engineer, or the AI assistant, at a point of change. Existing cybersecurity ontologies largely model attacks, indicators, and risk for detection and analysis, not the engineering-practice substance one must act on. This paper presents a use case for an existing bounded application-security ontology, AppSec Core, whose construction and validation are reported separately. We show how it is used. It makes the engineering-actionable fraction of those authorities addressable as a typed working set: the control objectives that apply, the practices that realize them, the mechanisms that implement them, and the evidence artifacts they expect, each traceable to the sources that justify it. We reach that working set from two entry points that recur in practice. Forward, from a code change: a change to authentication middleware scopes to its governing domain slice and returns the obligations the change must satisfy. Inverse, from a normative obligation: "make this NIS2-compliant" resolves a generic legal duty into the concrete engineering obligations it implies across slices, surfacing precisely the fraction of a mostly-governance regulation that lands in code. The same working set is what a human engineer reads and what an LLM-grounded assistant is handed as grounding. The use turns "read every applicable authority" into "satisfy this typed working set", for a code change or a compliance duty alike. The contribution is the demonstrated use; the artefact, its validation, and its governance are companion work.
item.dc:creator: Pedro Farinha

item.title: Side-Channel Attack Prevention for Post Quantum Cryptography Algorithms: A 3D-Shield Approach
item.description: arXiv:2611.01144v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Despite their theoretical quantum attack resistance, practical implementations of post-quantum cryptography (PQC) algorithms remain susceptible to side-channel attacks. This includes all standard algorithms selected the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) such as Kyber/ML-KEM, Dilithium/ML-DSA, Falcon/FN-DSA and SPHINCS+/SLH-DSA. This paper proposes an alternative defense for side-channel resilience based on 3D integration that uses 3D hardware to shield the underlying cryptographic activity by introducing decoy keys and physical shielding through stacking. The proposed approach can complement other security measures (such as masking and shuffling) on protecting Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) that move computation to dedicated NTT chips. We outline the construction of our approach and validate the effectiveness on a generic attack targeting intermediate computation inside an NTT butterfly.
item.dc:creator: Carl Benda, Eren Kurshan, Aydin Aysu, Paul Franzon

item.title: Enhancing Edge AI System Security with a Stacked Hardware Security Controller for Robust and Energy-Efficient Anomaly Detectio
item.description: arXiv:2611.01150v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In recent years, the growing adoption of Edge AI systems has been accompanied by a surge in security threats. Edge AI deployments face an rapidly evolving spectrum of security threats, from side-channel information leakage to ad- versarial model manipulation and physical device tampering. Conventional security mechanisms such as malware scanners and resource-intensive firewall solutions are unsuitable due to edge AIs typically limited computational resources, strict energy budgets and thermal constraints especially in battery-powered and field-deployed environments. This paper proposes a stacked, hardware-based security mechanism that enables low-overhead, continuous detection of anomalous execution patterns. Anomaly detection utilizing hard- ware performance counters and physical sensors outperforms software-based alternatives by providing key capabilities such as tamper-resistant root-of-trust isolation, negligible runtime overhead, and resilience against compromised operating systems. Experimental analysis shows that adversarial or malicious ap- plications produce observable deviations in sensor and thermal readings on Edge AI systems and hardware-based anomaly detection provides effective and low-overhead anomaly detection.
item.dc:creator: Carl Benda, Eren Kurshan, Paul Franzon

item.title: A Large-Scale Evaluation of Cookie Notice Privacy and Accessibility for Blind and Low Vision Users
item.description: arXiv:2611.01211v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present the first large-scale privacy and accessibility evaluation of cookie notices across 2,061 domains for blind and low vision (BLV) users. Using a Playwright-based crawler, a custom NVDA screen reader add-on, and the Lighthouse and WAVE accessibility tools, we measure UK GDPR/PECR compliance, tracker activity across pre-interaction, post-accept, and post-reject phases, and cookie notice accessibility for screen reader users. We find that 51 % of sites display a cookie notice, of which (at least) 50 % violate UK GDPR/PECR requirements. Accepting a notice produces a mean five-fold increase in tracker activity, and degrades page landmark structure on one in five sites. While 95 % of notices are readable by a screen reader, only 37 % carry a meaningful title, 39 % are announced immediately on page load, and 42 % use descriptive button labels. We reveal a systemic correlation: cookie notices failing legal privacy requirements disproportionately exhibit the weakest screen reader accessibility. This compounding privacy burden on BLV users demands urgent intervention from developers, regulators, and standards bodies.
item.dc:creator: James M. Clarke, Maryam Mehrnezhad

item.title: Optimal Conversion from Zero-Concentrated to Gaussian Differential Privacy
item.description: arXiv:2611.01218v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) and zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) are two competing privacy accounting frameworks, but they share similar minimax lower bounds in various estimation problems. Moreover, it is known that a mechanism satisfying $\mu$-GDP satisfies $(\mu^2/2)$-zCDP, whereas the converse fails to hold at the same calibration. In this paper, we establish the optimal reverse conversion, showing that every $\rho$-zCDP mechanism satisfies $\mu_{\mathrm{zCDP}}(\rho)$-GDP, where $\mu_{\mathrm{zCDP}}(\rho)=2\Phi^{-1}((1+e^{-t_\rho})^{-1})$ and $t_\rho$ uniquely solves the equation $\rho=t_\rho\tanh(t_\rho/2)$. We also obtain simplified bounds $\sqrt{\pi\rho}\leq\mu_{\mathrm{zCDP}}(\rho)\leq\sqrt{8\rho}$, with sharp constants, which imply equivalence of the two frameworks up to constants. This explains why their minimax risks agree up to a constant rescaling of the privacy budget. We show that the squared conversion is strictly convex, which implies that converting zCDP to GDP before applying composition or group privacy yields a tighter GDP guarantee than converting afterward. We also derive the sharp conversion from bounded-range and logistic DP mechanisms (e.g., exponential mechanism) to GDP, where converting before composition but after group privacy gives the tighter guarantee.
item.dc:creator: Yu-Wei Chen, Aaradhya Pandey, Jordan Awan

item.title: When Benign Is Unverified: Label-Signal Mismatch and Abstention-First Triage in Graph-Based Memory Forensics
item.description: arXiv:2611.01225v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine-learning triage for memory forensics is usually validated on corpora whose benign class is asserted by provenance and never verified. We report a validation study of a graph-based triage pipeline for Windows memory images: Volatility 3 output is compiled into typed heterogeneous graphs and scored by a temperature-scaled GINE classifier and two one-class encoders, fused with rule risk under an abstention gate. On MalVol-25 a transparent rule layer contradicts the benign label on every control (15/15 and 18/18 flagged; at least 11 of 15 paired controls rated HIGH or CRITICAL), and mean injection and command-and-control counts run higher on controls than on infected captures. We call this rule-label discordance label-signal mismatch; it shows the benign class is unverified, not compromised. Leave-one-family-out AUROC over matched pairs is provably three-valued, so a reported mean and standard deviation identify the fold composition. The learned model (0.786 +- 0.311; 9/4/1, scored in-sample by a frozen checkpoint) equals a logistic model over rule-derived attributes (0.786 +- 0.410; 11/0/3) in mean only, and its significance rests on dropping four saturated ties. The fusion path sends 97.7% of snapshots to analyst review, 95.3% with every gate disabled. Two public feature-level corpora show the same defect: on CIC-MalMem-2022 every benign row carries injected regions and one host-population feature reaches AUROC 0.997 under leave-one-family-out validation; on the Sihwail et al. (2021) sample the injection indicator fires on 53% of benign rows. We close with seven reporting artefacts for learned triage on corpora whose ground truth is asserted.

item.title: Bilinear Hulls for Support Splitting: Characterization, Optimization, and Applications
item.description: arXiv:2611.01337v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sendrier's Support Splitting Algorithm (SSA) is the standard solver for the Permutation Equivalence Problem (PEP); its cost is dominated by a term that grows exponentially in the hull dimension. We study, mathematically, how much this cost can be lowered by replacing the standard inner product, on which the hull is defined, with an alternative bilinear form. Two structural results give a complete answer: only a narrow two-parameter family of bilinear forms produces a hull on which SSA can still operate, namely those whose matrix in the standard basis is a linear combination of the identity and the all-ones matrix; and even within this family the hull dimension drops by at most one (with the reduction achieved on every self-dual code whose length is coprime to the field characteristic). Together, these results give a tight upper bound: since SSA on a code with hull dimension $h$ has cost dominated by $q^h$, replacing the standard hull with $\mathrm{Hull}_M$ lowers this dominant term from $q^h$ to at best $q^{h-1}$, so no bilinear-form generalization of the inner product can reduce the SSA cost by more than a factor of $q$, the field size. Going beyond this requires invariants outside the bilinear framework. As an application, we verify that PEP-based SPECK admits the factor-$q$ cost reduction, while LEP-based LESS and PKP-based PERK lie outside our framework. A SageMath implementation of the bilinear-hull preprocessing confirms feasibility at SPECK's recommended length $n = 252$.
item.dc:creator: Yusuke Aikawa, Keita Ishizuka, Tomoki Moriya

item.title: J-Anchor: Defending Against Prefill Attacks via J-Space Selective Refusal Restoration
item.description: arXiv:2611.01342v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prefill jailbreaks can cause safety-aligned language models to continue an unsafe assistant prefix even when they would refuse the same request under normal decoding. We study how the model's internal harmfulness and refusal signals evolve along this attacker-controlled trajectory. Using the Jacobian lens, we track vocabulary-grounded harmfulness and refusal signals from the assistant header through prefilling and subsequent generation. We identify a characteristic phenomenon, which we call refusal-state erosion: both the refusal signal and the harmfulness signal weaken as the prefill progresses, but the refusal signal progressively declines to the benign baseline by the end of the prefill, while the harmfulness signal remains above its benign baseline and detectable during subsequent generation. Motivated by this observation, we introduce J-Anchor, a training-free inference-time defense that uses the model's pre-attack harmfulness and refusal signals as a request-specific anchor and selectively restores weakened refusal in J-space during prefilling and decoding. J-Anchor substantially reduces attack success under both fixed and deep prefill attacks across different model families. J-Anchor largely preserves benign behavior and reasoning ability, and ablations highlight the importance of targeted restoration in the J-space refusal subspace. Our results suggest that preserving latent refusal dynamics offers a promising route to robust defense against prefill jailbreaks.
item.dc:creator: Running Yang, Beidi Zhao, Xiaoxiao Li

item.title: CipherFlow: Compiling AI Programs for Efficient Cryptographically Secure Inference
item.description: arXiv:2611.01450v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cryptographically secure inference faces two practical challenges: making secure programming accessible to AI developers and data scientists, and achieving efficient execution across deployment environments. Developers must compose cryptographic primitives correctly, while performance depends on hardware, networks, and evolving ciphertext states. We present CipherFlow, a compiler framework that takes a high-level AI computation graph, available cryptographic primitives, and a target hardware and network configuration to generate an executable, latency-optimized secure inference program. CipherFlow automates cryptographic execution decisions through three techniques: MicroBench profiles deployment-specific primitive costs; state-expanded planning jointly optimizes homomorphic encryption (HE) and secure multi-party computation (MPC) placement, conversions, and ciphertext maintenance under cryptographic-state constraints; and BlockFold summarizes branched regions to scale planning to Transformer graphs. Evaluation using measured HE/MPC backend costs across CPU/GPU and network settings shows up to 16.5$\times$ speedup on BERT-base and over 22$\times$ on ViT compared with static hybrid placement baselines. CipherFlow separates model programming from cryptographic execution decisions, enabling developers to express AI computations while the compiler constructs efficient secure programs.
item.dc:creator: Hedong Zhang, Mengxin Zheng, Qian Lou

item.title: Detecting Generated-Depth Injection Attacks on RGB-D Place Authentication
item.description: arXiv:2611.01550v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Advances in monocular depth estimation (MDE) now let an attacker generate depth from publicly available RGB images and submit forged RGB-D queries. Such attacks break a core assumption of RGB-D place authentication: that depth comes from a sensor. We study a presentation attack detection (PAD) classifier that uses geometric consistency between the enrollment and query views, as a software-layer defense. A three-stage evaluation shows how far this classifier detects software-injected depth, depending on how accurately the attacker knows the camera intrinsics. In the first stage, the attacker has only an estimate of the intrinsics, and the PAD classifier separates forgeries generated by all three MDE models with a validation area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.997-0.999. In the second stage, the attacker obtains the exact intrinsics, and the original PAD classifier falls to near chance (AUC 0.54-0.61); a retrained PAD classifier, however, still has the registration residual between enrollment and query as a cue. In the third stage, an oracle evaluation, in which the evaluator fits warps using the ground-truth 3D geometry, shows that detection falls to near chance only in its strongest case, where every valid query keypoint is given its ground-truth 3D coordinate. Of the detection cues, the reprojection error captures the attacker's misestimate of the intrinsics, whereas the registration residual remains even when the attacker knows the exact intrinsics.
item.dc:creator: Seigo Kawachi, Satoshi Matsuura

item.title: StateGate: A Behavioral-Fidelity Prompt Optimization Method for Long-Chain LLM Agents
item.description: arXiv:2611.01585v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Currently, long-chain LLM agents commonly suffer from behavioral degradation in complex tasks, where prompts are written in full but steps are not executed in full. To address this issue, existing approaches face three major challenges. First, constraints are strongly bound to their textual carriers; once natural-language constraint sentences are removed, their binding force vanishes. Second, the execution process lacks independent verification, as the evidence for judgment is often supplied by the executing party itself, leading to the failure of self-referential validation. Third, existing remediation schemes are difficult to generalize, and hard-coded mechanisms cannot be transferred across tasks. In this paper, we propose StateGate, a novel prompt-optimization scheme that transforms semantic constraints into symbolic gates enforced by an external deterministic runtime. By decoupling the content of a constraint from its carrier of efficacy, StateGate achieves behavioral fidelity in long-chain tasks without losing the binding force of the prompt. Specifically, we first propose four independent compression strategies (deduplication, generalization, externalization, and text-to-gating) together with their corresponding decision chains, enabling principled prompt symbolization. Second, we design a three-component architecture consisting of a state file, a validator, and an orchestrator, which thoroughly separates judgment authority from execution authority. Third, we formally prove that the compliance of symbolic constraints is independent of context size. Finally, we validate the framework on a vulnerability-discovery task in the security domain; the results show that StateGate achieves 100% execution closure and accurate vulnerability detection.
item.dc:creator: Shicheng Huang, Cai Fu, Jianqiang Lyu, Yifan Zhang, Xianmao Ji

item.title: Attack Patterns in Cross-chain Bridges: A Trust-based Empirical Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2611.01587v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid growth of multiple blockchain ecosystems has made cross-chain bridges essential for transferring assets and information across independent blockchains. Their multi-component architectures, cross-chain trust assumptions, and concentration of valuable assets expose them to diverse security threats. This paper presents an empirical study of cross-chain bridge attacks based on 48 evidence-supported real-world incidents from January 2022 to August 2026. We propose a behaviour-based attack pattern architecture comprising six trust-violation attack patterns, each defined by the primary trust assumption violated by the attacker: Proof Forgery,Logic Exploitation, Event Injection, Economic-State Manipulation, Credential Seizure, and Infrastructure Hijacking. The architecture further maps these patterns to five functional domains of cross-chain bridges: Deposit, Relay, Verification, Execution, and Governance and Operations, separating how a trust assumption is violated from where the compromised trust boundary lies. The 48 incidents correspond to $2.676 billion in gross bridge-specific losses, with the ten largest incidents accounting for 92.4% of total losses. Measured on the primary loss basis, Proof Forgery and Credential Seizure make up 86.2% of all losses, and the Verification and Governance and Operations domains hold 93.9%. A handful of very large incidents drives this concentration, yet it still holds when we switch to other loss bases or reclassify the boundary cases. By tying what attackers do to the bridge functions and security assumptions they target, the architecture gives threat modelling for cross-chain bridges an empirical footing.
item.dc:creator: Ishraq Samiha, Yasir Rahman, Rahma Mukta

item.title: Reddit Community Signals as a Supplementary Domain-Reputation Feature in Spam Classification: A Conservative Controlled Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2611.01813v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Email spam and phishing remain persistent threats, and purely algorithmic classifiers may struggle with unfamiliar senders, evolving message content, and cold-start domains. This study evaluates whether Reddit-derived community signals can serve as a supplementary domain-reputation feature in email spam classification. We use a preprocessed SpamAssassin-derived corpus of 5,582 emails and compare three feature configurations: (1) a baseline using TF-IDF and structural features; (2) a traditional-enhanced configuration adding urgency and action scores; and (3) a Reddit-enhanced configuration adding a binary discussion-presence indicator, a keyword-based Reddit score, and an urgency-Reddit interaction term. We train Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and Support Vector Machine models. In the preliminary single-split evaluation, the Random Forest model with Reddit-enhanced features achieves 97.94% accuracy, a 0.55 percentage-point improvement over the baseline, although the improvement is not statistically significant in the primary test split. Logistic Regression performance declines when additional features are introduced, and the SVM performs poorly and is treated as a negative control. Reddit signals appear most informative for rare domains, but approximately 70% of emails receive no Reddit-derived signal. Because the Reddit data are temporally later than the email corpus, we do not interpret the results as evidence of real-time detection. Instead, the study provides a conservative evaluation of community-derived signals as a supplementary, asynchronous domain-reputation feature and identifies the additional validation required before production deployment, including domain-grouped validation, temporally aligned contemporary data, and adversarial robustness testing.
item.dc:creator: Fatima Salcedo, Jide Edu

item.title: CertClaim: Towards Certified Model-Claim Verification for Coding-Agent Services
item.description: arXiv:2611.01950v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding-agent services are priced by the model they claim, making the verification of such model claims crucial for their users. In this paper, we reveal that existing model auditing methods rely on a latent assumption that the deployment is static, i.e., the claimed model is always served in one reference configuration. This assumption does not hold for coding-agent services, whose providers may legitimately change the sampling preset, the reasoning mode or the system prompt without changing the model. As a result, existing methods either falsely accuse honest providers or miss cheap derivatives of the claimed model. To address this problem, we propose a certified model-claim verification method (dubbed CertClaim). Instead of testing the service against one reference deployment, we make the authorized deployments part of the claim and test whether some authorized deployment explains all the evidence of the service, by calibrating multiple evidence channels in every authorized deployment and fusing them within each deployment. We provide theoretical analyses of its false-accusation rate and detection condition. Extensive experiments on eight claims, two agent harnesses and three task suites verify the effectiveness of CertClaim, which is valid in every setting while separating substitutes far better than existing methods, as well as its resistance to potential adaptive attacks.
item.dc:creator: Jiacheng Lu, Qixuan Yang, Tao Song, Daxin Jiang, Jing Li, Zuo Bai, Haibing Guan

item.title: Step-Zero Attack: Agent Safety Before Observability
item.description: arXiv:2611.01953v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing attacks and defenses for coding agents act once content enters the model context: injected text persuades the model, and guards inspect what the model reads. Yet to judge whether processing an unknown archive, network response, or image is safe, an agent often must process it first, and that step can do harm before any content reaches the model. We call this first processing Step Zero, and harm done by it a Step-Zero attack. Across seven harnesses and six models, each agent received only a path or URL to a crafted input, paired with a benign twin showing the same visible fields. Step Zero is where most agents are already unsafe: 32/42 harness-model pairs overran a 4 MiB disk budget, 26/42 before the model saw any member, and four of the six models did so in every round (84/84), so the damage precedes any model-side defense. Every twin stayed within budget, so the attacker's bytes alone cause the harm. On network and image inputs the risk moves to what the agent writes: agents stored the body under the name the input declared, letting the input decide what is written, and their checks faded once cues were removed. Model-free tests trace the harm to the processing primitive, so we defend it there: a gate that counts the bytes each call produces held every routed extraction within budget while agents completed 25/28 tasks. Vendors should pair such gates with safety-alignment training that teaches agents to inspect an input before processing it.
item.dc:creator: Tian Qin, Yuhang Jiang, Junzhe Chen, Lit Sin Tan, Lijie Wen

item.title: Beyond Prompt Injection: The Tool Update Gap in LLM Agent Security
item.description: arXiv:2611.01976v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model based agents increasingly rely on external tools to invoke services and interact with web resources. These tools can evolve through software updates, yet agentic frameworks may continue trusting them without re-verifying their safety after implementation changes. This tool update gap creates a supply-chain vulnerability in agentic systems: because updated tool code executes outside the LLM's context window, malicious functionality embedded in tool updates can bypass defenses centered on model-visible interactions, leaving agents exposed to stealthy, persistent threats that existing in-context defenses can hardly address. To thoroughly investigate this threat, we introduce ETUDE (Exploiting Tool Updates for Direct Execution), an attack that embeds malicious functionality into updates of initially benign tools to produce compromised tools, while preserving their legitimate tool functionality. Unlike prompt-based attacks, ETUDE operates entirely outside the LLM's context and requires no adversarial instructions, thereby bypassing defenses restricted to model-visible content. We evaluate ETUDE across three representative attack workloads and seven widely used commercial and open-source agentic frameworks, including Gemini CLI, Codex CLI, and Claude Code. The results show that ETUDE achieves a 97.6% ASR while maintaining a 95.9% legitimate task completion rate. We further examine existing defenses and find that they provide insufficient protection against this threat. These findings expose a fundamental blind spot in current agent security practices: trust established for a tool does not necessarily remain valid after its implementation updates.
item.dc:creator: Shiyu Kan (Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China), Yue Qi (Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China), Yufei Han (Inria, Rennes, France), Xinjian Luo (Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China), Guojun Xiong (Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China), Xiaofeng Gao (Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China)

item.title: Accelerating QUIC Encryption in WebAssembly Using WASM-SIMD
item.description: arXiv:2611.01989v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: WebAssembly (Wasm) runs untrusted code in a portable, lightweight sandbox and is increasingly used to host services on shared servers and edge platforms. Running the QUIC transport protocol inside Wasm would let each application choose and update its own transport without changing the host. QUIC, however, encrypts every packet, and Wasm offers neither dedicated AES instructions nor carry-less multiplication; a Wasm QUIC stack has been reported to reach only 17.6% of native goodput, with cryptography as its largest cost. Whether the 128-bit SIMD extension of Wasm (WASM-SIMD) can recover this cost, and what limits a pure-Wasm stack once it does, has remained unclear. Here we show that explicit WASM-SIMD kernels recover much of the cryptographic cost, after which non-cryptographic costs become the limit. On two hosts connected by 10-Gigabit Ethernet, kernels that process eight AES blocks or four ChaCha20 blocks per pass raise receiver goodput over a non-SIMD baseline by 61.34% for AES-128-GCM and 31.55% for ChaCha20-Poly1305, whereas compiler auto-vectorization gains only 1.28% for AES-128-GCM. ChaCha20-Poly1305 still delivers 1.99 times the goodput of AES-128-GCM, confirming end to end the preference that stand-alone cipher benchmarks suggest. Receiver-side profiling combined with Amdahl's law predicts that even native-speed cryptography would leave Wasm at roughly one third of the goodput of the fastest native stack. Cryptographic acceleration is therefore necessary but not sufficient: memory allocation, runtime overhead and per-datagram UDP I/O now bound pure-Wasm transports. We anticipate that this per-category cost breakdown will guide further optimization of Wasm network stacks and the design of system interfaces for batched I/O.
item.dc:creator: Sota Yamawaki, Yasuo Okabe

item.title: One String to Rule Them All: Measuring Consent Under the IAB Global Privacy Platform
item.description: arXiv:2611.02014v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many privacy regulations, including the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA), require websites to honor users' opt-out choices. To facilitate this process, industry has introduced technical standards such as the IAB Global Privacy Platform (GPP), which aims to standardize collection and transmission of user consent information across multiple jurisdictions. However, it remains unclear whether these standards consistently and correctly transmit user opt-out choices, or whether opt-out choices are respected by advertisers. In this study, we conduct an in-depth analysis of consent propagation under the GPP framework. We collect data from four web crawls across four experimental settings to analyze how widely the standard is adopted, the extent to which opt-out signals propagate from publishers to third parties, and whether these signals reach and alter third-party advertiser behavior. Our analysis reveals several inconsistencies in the implementation and adoption of the standard that result in user consent signals being lost and user opt-out choices not being respected by the advertisers.
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Abu Bakar Aziz, Christo Wilson

item.title: Query-efficient scan-and-search watermark localization
item.description: arXiv:2611.02030v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recently, the detection of AI-generated content has been of particular importance in various fields of our society. For accountability purposes, many large language models (LLMs) have implicitly watermarked their outputs. Localizing such watermarks requires a piece of text to undergo an additional verification process. Existing localization methods typically rely on dense token-level scoring, making verification costly even when an LLM-generated watermark only sparsely appears. To tackle this problem, we design a new adaptive allocation strategy that first maintains broad document coverage and then progressively concentrates the detection budget on regions that exhibit stronger watermark evidence or are more likely to contain watermarked content. We then transform the statistical signals from the selected regions into e-values and employ the proposed token-weighted e-BH procedure to determine the localized watermark regions. The resulting framework is called BELL (Budgeted E-evidence Localization for LLM Watermarks). Theoretically, BELL can control the token-weighted false discovery rate (FDR) without independence assumptions across regions. Finally, extensive experimental results demonstrate that BELL consistently outperforms competing methods across multiple LLMs, datasets, and watermarking schemes.
item.dc:creator: Liyuan Wang, Xinsong Ma, Ziye Ma

item.title: SANAI: Secure ECC Distributed Keyed Parity Embedded in Weights for Protecting Neural Networks against Bit-Flip Attacks
item.description: arXiv:2611.02042v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantized neural networks store weights in dense memory, where bit flips caused by voltage scaling, aging, radiation, or deliberate attacks such as RowHammer can severely degrade model behavior. A single corrupted high-order bit can cause misclassifications or nonsensical language-model outputs. Embedded error-correcting codes (ECC) avoid dedicated parity storage by hiding parity within model weights, but existing schemes embed uniformly across layers and bit planes, leave parity unsecured, and tolerate bit-error rates (BERs) only up to about 6%. An adversary aware of sensitive weights and the ECC scheme can also bypass protection by exceeding the correction capability of targeted codewords. We propose SANAI, a sensitivity-guided, bit-plane-selective scheme that protects critical model weights against bit flips with zero additional parity-storage overhead. SANAI secures parity through keyed embedding across a two-dimensional weight space: spread-transform dither modulation binds parity to a secret key, and keyed interleaving disperses concentrated attacks across codewords. We derive a survival law showing that robustness is governed by the correctable fraction t/n rather than by t alone, and a closed-form bound on the protectable fraction of a model. As a streaming checker on an 8x8 systolic array, SANAI verifies weights on the load path with 0.41% area overhead and no additional memory. Across ten vision backbones, three quantization schemes, and ten language models from 82M to 13B parameters, SANAI stays within about one percentage point of clean accuracy at BERs up to 12%, twice the maximum of prior embedded-ECC approaches. It survives fine-tuning bit-exactly, neutralizes progressive and targeted bit-flip attacks, and exactly corrects AttentionBreaker and SilentStriker attacks.
item.dc:creator: Habibur Rahaman, Daniel Lobo, Md Rezoan Ferdous, Swarup Bhunia

item.title: ZT-DAC: ML-Driven Dynamic Access Control Policy for Zero Trust in DER Networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.02107v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The increasing penetration of Distributed Energy Resources (DERs) in the smart grid has significantly expanded the cyber-attack surface. Traditionally, DER networks rely on static role-based access control (RBAC) mechanisms that assume persistent trust after authentication. This limitation enables adversaries to maintain unauthorized privileges and move laterally across DER systems, disrupting grid operations. Although attribute-based access control (ABAC) enables fine-grained and context-aware access decisions, it does not fully eliminate implicit trust. Zero Trust (ZT) principles can be incorporated to enhance ABAC policies. This paper proposes a dynamic access control framework for implementing ZT in DER networks (ZT-DAC). The proposed solution employs a two-stage verification process and integrates an Open Policy Agent (OPA)-based RBAC with a machine learning (ML)-based ABAC to enforce continuous and adaptive trust score assessment. To support realistic DER operations, a DER-specific access control model is developed and used to generate a domain-informed dataset of access requests incorporating both legitimate and adversarial behaviors. Experimental results on the dataset show that the OPA-based decision layer achieves \(91.92\%\) accuracy, with a False Positive Rate of \(14.45\%\), while the ML model achieves a Mean Absolute Error of \(2.074\) and an \(R^2\) of \(0.891\) in trust-score prediction. The ABAC layer achieves \(93.27\%\) accuracy, with a FPR of \(3.88\%\), validating its practical feasibility within realistic DER environments.
item.dc:creator: Arun B. Chandrasekaran, Damilola Popoola, Souradeep Bhattacharya, Manimaran Govindarasu

item.title: Bounded Retained History in a Proxy Flow Replay: A Mixed Predictive Pilot and an Allocation Study
item.description: arXiv:2611.02123v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We examine bounded retained history through a frozen predictive pilot and a subsequent allocation study on a curated UNSW-NB15 flow mirror. Both use an artificial release-order replay based on raw ltime ticks, with equal-tick records querying a shared prior-group state. In the pilot, the model with added retained relational features had lower reconnaissance recall than the current-flow-plus-counters baseline (43.66% versus 47.84%) and lower benign false-positive rate (3.63% versus 6.68%) at separately frozen operating thresholds, together with lower AUROC. This mixed result did not establish a predictive advantage. A development-only audit subsequently found that capacity eviction dominated expiration in the 256-record, 300-tick FIFO state, with a median completed record lifetime of 11 ticks. A protocol specified before its single execution, but after the pilot and post-hoc mechanism audit, compared five label-blind retention arms on the already-used development trace. Its primary equal-source endpoint averaged retained/reference ratios for service-expanded source out-degree and source-destination service diversity. Source-balanced retention at 256 records exceeded FIFO-256 by a pooled endpoint difference of 0.440738 and met the prespecified materiality and subblock rule. Crucially, the event-weighted ratios for both quantities decreased relative to FIFO-256: the result is specific to the equal-source weighting objective and does not establish uniformly improved retention. The study supplies neither evidence of detection improvement nor an explanation of the pilot result. Reused data, concentrated reconnaissance support, proxy timing, and the absence of a qualified independent corpus bound the interpretation.
item.dc:creator: Juan S. Santillana

item.title: Black-Box Adversarial Example Attacks on Machine Learning based Election Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.02166v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine learning models have shown exceptional accuracy for ballot classification in election systems. Recent research has demonstrated that these ballot classification models are vulnerable to adversarial example attacks. This is a critical security issue because a successful attack could alter the outcome of an election and undermine the democratic process. However, all adversarial example attacks in the voting domain have assumed a white-box threat model, where the classifier parameters are known. In this work, we advance the field of machine learning in election systems by analyzing a realistic black-box adversary. We implement and evaluate eleven state-of-the-art black-box attacks: query based attacks ADBA, Square, SurFree, RayS, and SA-MOO. We also test adaptive transfer based black-box attacks with APGD-$l_\infty$, APGD-$l_2$, APGD-$l_1$, PGD $l_0$, PGD $l_0$+$l_\infty$, and PGD $l_0$+$\sigma$. Our attacks span multiple different norms ($l_\infty$, $l_2$, $l_1$, and $l_0$) and three different black-box adversarial threat models (decision based, score based and transfer based). In addition to digital analyses, we physically print and scan $20,000$ adversarial examples to evaluate the real-world performance of different black-box attacks. Our finding demonstrate an even larger physical-digital robustness gap exists for black-box adversarial examples than for white-box adversarial examples. Lastly, we conduct the first ever adversarial example transferability study in the voting domain and test adversarial training and barrier zones as two possible black-box defense strategies.
item.dc:creator: Subek Acharya, Syed Ayon, Khaleque Md Aashiq Kamal, Alina Barnett, Surya Eada, Kaleel Mahmood

item.title: A Matched Evaluation of QUBO Action Models and Defensive Remediation in Cyber Attack Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.02179v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study examines how vulnerability-specific actions affect quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) models for minimum-cost cyber attack paths and defensive remediation. Edge-flow and variable-length hop formulations are evaluated using simulated annealing, steepest descent, and tabu search against exact classical references. Experiments on six independent synthetic topologies separate the effects of transition eligibility, vulnerability labels, exploit costs, and multiple exploit alternatives. A single labeled action per eligible transition preserves feasible paths, optimal costs, and QUBO size. Under the tested settings, multiple exploit alternatives were associated with approximately unchanged valid-path recovery, lower optimal-path recovery, and substantially larger representations, particularly for the hop formulation. These recovery differences remain descriptive because they are not statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons. An evaluation on a published 3CX attack graph with synthetic costs demonstrates applicability beyond the generated topologies. The defensive extension selects patches within a budget to raise attack-path costs to specified thresholds or disconnect protected targets. Against exhaustive and mixed-integer references, the tested QUBO heuristics recovered an optimal patch set in 12 of 16 calls across eight scenarios on one topology. The results characterize formulation correctness, solution recovery, and resource requirements using classical local optimization, without establishing quantum computational advantage.
item.dc:creator: Kasymkhan Khubiev, Yaroslav Kholodov, Alexey S. Petrenko

item.title: Increasing the security of advanced metering infrastructure using dynamic defense methods
item.description: arXiv:2611.02193v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With the increase in Internet usage over the last half century, technology has also benefited from the growth and development of the Internet. It is no wonder that smart grids are emerging as one of the most popular technologies of today. As smart grids are connected to the internet, they are constantly vulnerable to cyberattacks. It is always possible for attackers to gain access to metering system infrastructure which is a major and critical part of smart grids. When this system is not working properly because of some security threats, irreparable damage is in the place for a country and its industries. This article suggests utilizing dynamic Applications that Participate in Their Own Defense defenses to secure such systems and infrastructures.
item.dc:creator: Mohsen Saffar, Hamid Reza Naji

item.title: Detect, Repair and Audit: A Hierarchical Multi-Agent Defense Against Adversarial Attacks in Energy Forecasting
item.description: arXiv:2611.02310v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate electricity-demand forecasting is essential for the modern energy infrastructure. Recently, Times-Series Large Language Models (TS-LLMs) have emerged as a promising approach to forecasting more accurate demand from historical consumption data in zero- and few-shot settings, helping energy operators effectively plan supply and allocate energy resources. However, these models are vulnerable to compromised sensor inputs that can distort forecasts and lead to erroneous market orders or unnecessary load shedding. Existing defenses focus primarily on end-device forecasting, overlooking the distinct data-drift, latency, and audit requirements across energy infrastructure. To address this gap, we extract from major energy standards and regulatory frameworks a three-layer conceptual model that captures the security postures for each layer. Guided by this model, we develop a Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) detector coupled with signal repair at local control centers, designed to mitigate distributional data drift through complementary feature-based detection and clean-reference-calibrated repair while meeting latency budgets. We further deploy an evidence-grounded LLM auditing agent with human-in-the-loop validation for audit-critical Virtual Power Plants (VPPs). In our evaluation, the best MARL configuration achieves an F1 score above 0.91 across all dataset-attack pairs, while signal repair reduces adversarial-to-clean input Relative Squared Error (RSE) by up to 83%. The few-shot auditor detects 77.78% of attacks in the Sherlock dataset. On the evaluated hardware, detection and repair require 7.95 ms on average, with a worst-observed latency of 14.50 ms, remaining within the local-center latency budget informed by IEEE 1646.
item.dc:creator: Zewei Shi, Ruoxi Sun, Minhui Xue, Feng Liu, Hua Ma, Xingliang Yuan, Surya Nepal

item.title: Malware Clustering in the Wild: Taxonomy, Challenges, and Evaluation Metrics
item.description: arXiv:2611.02380v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As malware continues to grow in volume, diversity, and sophistication, clustering has emerged as a critical technique for analyzing large malware corpora. Clustering enables the discovery of structural relationships, behavioral patterns, and evolutionary trends, and is widely used to group unknown samples, infer malware family boundaries, and identify novel variants. However, existing research remains fragmented, employing a wide range of clustering techniques with no unified perspective that systematically organizes prior work or clearly identifies gaps in the literature. This survey addresses this gap by organizing previous malware clustering research into seven categories: centroid-based, hierarchical-based, density-based, distribution-based, mixed- type, fuzzy, and AI-driven approaches. In addition, this survey summarizes publicly available malware datasets commonly used in clustering research and examines the feature representations derived from these datasets. Our goal is to clarify the current landscape and outline promising avenues for future research on malware clustering, including how AI-driven methods may shape large-scale and reproducible analysis.
item.dc:creator: Raguvir S, Bojing Li, Prajna Bhandary, Charles Nicholas

item.title: Networked Synthetic Social Engineering on the Web
item.description: arXiv:2611.02407v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Several genuine AI services may repeat one unsupported source, and correcting that source may leave later reports unchanged. We examine these networked consequences of synthetic social engineering (SSE), deliberately misleading influence intended to redirect AI recipients from authorized objectives. Our framework connects social influence, information aggregation, and misinformation correction research to observable evidence and permission boundaries. It separates originating attempts from legitimate intermediaries' work and distinguishes identity, evidentiary support, and authorization. We test four relationships using Qwen3-4B and two briefing tasks across 1,080 research units in our Agent Service Exchange and Evidence Commons (ASE-EC). Multiple dependent publishers produced no supported increase in unsupported verification (78.3% versus 75.0%); publication availability left downstream violation reach at 40.0% in both arms. These comparisons direct attention to weaknesses already present in the reference workflows. High reference error rates and retained private handoffs preclude claims of immunity to social pressure. Without scope revalidation, corrections identifying dependent reports reduced residual invalid decisions from 14.4% to 8.1% at equal notification coverage and increased successful report repairs from 16/63 to 36/63. Scope revalidation added no demonstrated protection, and clearing dialogue offered no established recovery advantage. Unapproved requests persisted, all blocked by an external gateway. For designers, the findings caution against treating publisher count as independent evidence, notification as repair, or cleared histories as recovery. They support targeting corrections at reused reports, assessing factual and permission recovery separately, and enforcing authorization at execution.
