item.title: BioZero: Privacy-Preserving and Publicly Verifiable On-Chain Biometric Authentication via Homomorphic Commitments and Zero-Knowledge Proofs
item.description: arXiv:2409.17509v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Blockchain-based identity services let applications across administrative domains verify biometric authentication results without sharing a trusted biometric server. BioZero evaluates how to protect private templates while limiting on-chain execution and submitted transaction-data costs under explicit cryptographic assumptions. FullCheck provides knowledge soundness for the modular distance relation, but exhaustive coordinate checks cost 22.1 million gas at N=128 in a threshold-stand-in benchmark. SpotCheck tests a natural optimization: sampling checks within the same homomorphic structure. Checking seven coordinates saves 81.3% gas, reducing it to 4.1 million, but retains 127,844 bytes of calldata. We prove that changing one product commitment can shift the reconstructed distance to any chosen residue and evade a uniform sample of t among N coordinates with probability 1-t/N. Negligible attack success therefore requires nearly exhaustive checking, limiting the scope for coordinate-check savings. CircuitCheck changes the verification structure, proving commitment openings, coordinate ranges, and the integer distance threshold in one circuit. Its complete reference transaction costs 255 thousand gas with 356 bytes of calldata. At N=128, median proving time and process peak memory are 0.63 s and 822 MiB on the evaluated workstation. On two face datasets, every tested width of at least 6 bits stays within 0.46 percentage points of float accuracy, supporting the shared integer-input front end. These results favor CircuitCheck for the evaluated integer matching task in blockchain-backed cross-domain identity services, provided that committed probes are separately bound to authenticated live captures.
item.dc:creator: Zibin Lin, Taotao Wang, Junhao Lai, Shengli Zhang, Qing Yang, Soung Chang Liew

item.title: Software Security in Software-Defined Networking: A Systematic Literature Review
item.description: arXiv:2502.13828v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Software-defined networking (SDN) separates the control plane from the data plane and exposes the network through software applications and open APIs. The same programmability that drove its adoption also turned the network into a large body of software, and that software can be vulnerable. Knowing where and how SDN software fails is a prerequisite for defending it, yet the literature offers no consolidated account of the problem. We address this gap with a systematic literature review of 113 primary studies published between 2012 and 2025 on the security of the software that makes up SDN. We study how each software component becomes vulnerable, how attackers exploit it, which testing and analysis techniques expose its defects, and how the field has evolved. The review yields a taxonomy of vulnerabilities and attack vectors organized by SDN software component, a synthesis of the methods used to find software defects in each component, and a set of open problems that mark the most promising directions for future work. Earlier surveys treat SDN security as a networking problem; ours is, to our knowledge, the first to treat SDN components as software artifacts whose code, logic, and interactions can be defective. Our artifacts are available at https://github.com/mad975/SDNSoftwareSecurity_SLR.
item.dc:creator: Moustapha Awwalou Diouf, Samuel Ouya, Jacques Klein, Tegawend\'e F. Bissyand\'e

item.title: How Safe Are AI-Generated Patches? A Large-scale Study on Security Risks in LLM and Agentic Automated Program Repair on SWE-bench
item.description: arXiv:2507.02976v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) and agentic frameworks are increasingly used for development tasks such as automated program repair (APR). Prior work has identified security risks in LLM-generated code, but most studies focus on synthetic, simplified, or isolated tasks. We present a large-scale security analysis of LLM-generated patches using 20,000+ GitHub issues from SWE-bench. We evaluate developer-written patches, two standalone LLMs (Llama 3.3 Instruct-70B and GPT-5.4 nano), and four agentic frameworks (OpenHands, AutoCodeRover, HoneyComb, and SWE-agent). We also analyze code, issue, and project-level factors associated with insecure patches. Under our evaluated SWE-bench setup, Llama 3.3 introduced 135 manually confirmed vulnerabilities across the train and test sets, compared with 12 in developer-written patches for the same issues. On the SWE-bench test set, GPT-5.4 nano introduced 3 vulnerabilities compared with 2 in developer patches. All four evaluated agentic frameworks also introduced vulnerabilities. OpenHands had the highest retained count, with 44 vulnerabilities across 11 issue instances. Vulnerabilities are associated with broader code modifications and with issues missing specific information. These results suggest that APR systems require proactive risk assessment methods that consider both generated code and issue context.
item.dc:creator: Amirali Sajadi, Kostadin Damevski, Preetha Chatterjee

item.title: CISAF: A Framework for Risk Assessment of Academic and Research Cyberinfrastructure
item.description: arXiv:2509.00266v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Academic and research cyberinfrastructures (AR-CIs) present unique risk and security challenges due to their collaborative nature and heterogeneous components. However, the industry-well-accepted risk assessment approaches have limited compatibility and specificity for complex systems like cyberinfrastructures (CIs). We propose CyberInfrastructure Security Analysis Framework (CISAF) -- a simple, systematic, mission-centric, and integrable approach to file for CI risk assessment. CISAF serves as a plug-in to traditional risk assessment/management frameworks, a convenient tool to extrapolate the cybersecurity risks for complex cybersystems. It guides AR-CI administrators through a top-down process: (1) defining unacceptable losses, (2) identifying associated system hazards and critical assets, (3) analyzing possible attack paths targeting these critical assets, (4) cross-referencing security mechanisms deployed along these attack paths, and (5) integrating results into established risk assessment/management frameworks. By combining information about CI architecture, missions, attack graphs, and security mechanisms, CISAF provides actionable guidelines, structured views of high-priority security risks, and streamlined translation into established frameworks.
item.dc:creator: Qishen Sam Liang, Jelena Mirkovic, Brian Kocoloski

item.title: AgentTypo: Adaptive Typographic Prompt Injection Attacks against Black-box Multimodal Agents
item.description: arXiv:2510.04257v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multimodal agents built on large vision-language models are increasingly deployed in open-world settings but remain highly vulnerable to prompt injection. Typographic text-in-image attacks such as FigStep have been evaluated mainly on standalone vision-language models. For agents, user goals, webpage context, and action history make the effect of embedded instructions uncertain, and robustness to behavior-guided, adaptive visual injections remains insufficiently studied. We introduce AgentTypo, a black-box red-teaming framework that launches adaptive typographic prompt injection by embedding optimized text into webpage images. We formulate an attention-guided automatic typographic prompt-injection objective that favors the attacker's expected answer over the clean-page answer, together with task-conditioned visual attention from small question-answering models. A novel black-box optimization method searches text position, contrast, and color. To further strengthen the attack, we develop a multi-LLM system that iteratively refines injection prompts using evaluation feedback and retrieves successful past examples for strategy learning. Experiments on the VWA-Adv and Mind2Web benchmarks show that AgentTypo significantly outperforms state-of-the-art image-based prompt injection attacks. Across seven closed- and open-source model backends, AgentTypo-pro achieves 45%-83% ASR, outperforming the CLIP-based AgentAttack by 29-47% and previous typographic attacks by 25%-37% on VWA-Adv.
item.dc:creator: Yanjie Li, Yiming Cao, Dong Wang, Bin Xiao

item.title: AuthRank: Scoring Source Credibility to Counter Poisoning in CTI LLM Pipelines
item.description: arXiv:2510.20768v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) pipelines have become essential for processing Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) to quickly extract updated threat information from open source feeds and reports for real time processing. However, these pipelines are susceptible to poisoning attacks, and previously proposed defenses can fail for CTI contexts as cyber threat information is often completely novel, and attackers can easily mimic the stylistic conventions. We propose that the robustness of LLM pipelines can be improved by applying source credibility algorithms on document corpora, using PageRank as an example. We introduce AuthRank, a credibility score computed from citation networks built using explicit citations, LLM-inferred citations, and claim-level entailment, enhanced with time decay and author credibility. Our experiments on the standardized MS MARCO dataset demonstrate improved accuracy under poisoning, and we show proof-of-concept performance on CTI documents and feeds.
item.dc:creator: Austin Jia, Avaneesh Ramesh, Zain Shamsi, Daniel Zhang, Alex Liu

item.title: Lifefin: Escaping Mempool Explosions in DAG-based BFT
item.description: arXiv:2511.15936v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)-based Byzantine Fault-Tolerant (BFT) protocols have emerged as promising solutions for high-throughput blockchains. By decoupling data dissemination from transaction ordering and constructing a well-connected DAG in the mempool, these protocols enable zero-message ordering and implicit view changes. However, we identify a fundamental liveness vulnerability: an adversary can trigger mempool explosions to prevent transaction commitment, ultimately compromising the protocol's liveness. In response, this work presents Lifefin, a generic and self-stabilizing protocol designed to integrate seamlessly with existing DAG-based BFT protocols and circumvent such vulnerabilities. Lifefin leverages the Agreement on Common Subset (ACS) mechanism, allowing nodes to escape mempool explosions by committing transactions with bounded resource usage even in adverse conditions. As a result, Lifefin imposes (almost) zero overhead in typical cases while effectively eliminating liveness vulnerabilities. To demonstrate the effectiveness of Lifefin, we integrate it into two state-of-the-art DAG-based BFT protocols, Sailfish and Mysticeti, resulting in two enhanced variants: Sailfish-Lifefin and Mysticeti-Lifefin. We implement these variants and compare them with the original Sailfish and Mysticeti systems. Our evaluation demonstrates that Lifefin achieves comparable transaction throughput while introducing only minimal additional latency to resist similar attacks.
item.dc:creator: Jianting Zhang, Sen Yang, Alberto Sonnino, Sebasti\'an Loza, Aniket Kate

item.title: Trustworthy Blockchain-based Federated Learning for Electronic Health Records: Identity-Gated Participation against Sybil Attacks
item.description: arXiv:2602.02629v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Federated learning allows hospitals to train a shared clinical model without exchanging patient records, but its aggregation assumes that each participant is a distinct institution. In an open federation, an adversary can register many fake identities (a Sybil attack) and outweigh honest hospitals. Byzantine-robust aggregation mitigates such attacks only while the adversary is a minority. We ask whether binding participation to accountable institutional identity closes that gap, and at what cost. We present TBFL, a framework in which an accountable authority issues Verifiable Credentials to the Decentralized Identifiers of hospitals, and a smart-contract registry on a peer-to-peer ledger admits model updates only from credentialed senders. We evaluated a prototype on in-hospital mortality prediction with MIMIC-IV records split across simulated hospitals, comparing the identity gate with federated averaging, three robust aggregators, norm clipping, and a similarity-based defense. Robust aggregators held against a Sybil minority, and norm clipping only against random vectors; all failed when half the participants were Sybils trained on real records with flipped labels. The similarity-based defense stopped mutually similar Sybils but yielded to perturbed ones. The gate rejected all unauthorized submissions and maintained attack-free performance for every strategy up to 60% Sybils. It did not stop credentialed hospitals that flipped their own labels, whereas the gate followed by the coordinate-wise median withstood both. On a local node, on-chain checks added about 1% to training time; fees made training impractical on a public mainnet but affordable on a rollup. Identity gating complements robust aggregation rather than replacing it.
item.dc:creator: Rodrigo Tertulino, Ricardo Almeida, Laercio Alencar

item.title: Boost+: Equitable, Incentive-Compatible Block Building
item.description: arXiv:2602.04007v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Block space on the blockchain is scarce and must be allocated efficiently through block building. However, Ethereum's current block-building ecosystem, MEV-Boost, has become highly centralized due to integration, which distorts competition, reduces blockspace efficiency, and obscures MEV flow transparency. To improve equitability and economic efficiency in block building, we propose $\textsf{Boost+}$, a system that pools submitted order flows inside an attested execution environment and gives all participating block-building algorithms equal access to them. The core of $\textsf{Boost+}$ is the mechanism $M_{\textsf{Boost+}}$, built around a baseline block-building algorithm. $M_{\textsf{Boost+}}$ aligns incentives for both searchers (intermediaries that generate or route transactions) and builders: Truthful bidding is a dominant strategy for all builders. For searchers, truthful reporting is dominant whenever the baseline algorithm dominates competing builders, and it remains dominant for all conflict-free transactions, even when builders may win. We further show that even if a searcher can technically integrate with a builder, non-integration combined with truthful bidding still dominates any deviation for conflict-free transactions. We also implement a concrete baseline algorithm informed by empirical analysis of real-world transactions and evaluate its efficacy using historical data.
item.dc:creator: Mengqian Zhang, Sen Yang, Kartik Nayak, Fan Zhang

item.title: Explainability-Aware Evaluation of Transfer Learning Models for IoT DDoS Detection Under Resource Constraints
item.description: arXiv:2602.22488v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks threaten the availability of Internet of Things (IoT) infrastructures, especially in resource-constrained deployments. Although transfer learning models have shown promising detection accuracy, their reliability, computational feasibility, and interpretability in operational environments remain insufficiently explored. This study presents an explainability-aware empirical evaluation of seven pre-trained convolutional neural network architectures for multi-class IoT DDoS detection using the CICDDoS2019 dataset and an image-based traffic representation. The analysis integrates classification performance metrics, complementary statistical indicators (MCC, Cohen's kappa, and Youden Index), training and inference cost assessment, and interpretability evaluation using Grad-CAM and SHAP. Results indicate that DenseNet and MobileNet-based architectures achieve strong detection performance while demonstrating superior reliability and compact, class-consistent attribution patterns. MobileNet achieves the highest reported classification accuracy and several of the strongest reliability statistics, whereas DenseNet169 exhibits the most favorable qualitative interpretability characteristics based on Grad-CAM and SHAP. MobileNetV3 offers a potential trade-off between inference latency, classification performance, and qualitative interpretability for resource-constrained deployment. The findings emphasize the importance of combining performance, reliability, and explainability criteria when selecting deep learning models for IoT DDoS detection.
item.dc:creator: Nelly Elsayed

item.title: Clawdrain: Exploiting Tool-Calling Chains for Stealthy Token Exhaustion in OpenClaw Agents
item.description: arXiv:2603.00902v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Tool-calling LLM agents rely on third-party skills to extend their capabilities, but this openness exposes a supply-chain attack surface in which malicious skill instructions can manipulate agent execution across multiple turns. In this work, we present Clawdrain, a Trojanized OpenClaw skill that induces resource exhaustion through a Segmented Verification Process (SVP). SVP combines stateful progression, repair-driven repetition, and termination to create costly tool-calling chains while preserving a legitimate final payload. We evaluate Clawdrain in a production-like OpenClaw deployment with real API billing across Gemini 2.5 Pro, DeepSeek V4 Flash, and Claude Sonnet 4.6. Clawdrain achieves 2-16 times token amplification with plain SVP, while the three models exhibit distinct behaviors, including autoregressive compliance, proactive scripting, and extended trial-and-error reasoning. Our findings reveal that agent resource exhaustion arises not only from output generation, but also from repeated context re-ingestion, tool coordination, reasoning, and recovery, motivating system-level controls over cumulative skill behavior.
item.dc:creator: Ben Dong, Zhonghao Guo, Tianyi Li, Qian Wang

item.title: WebWeaver: Breaking Topology Confidentiality in LLM Multi-Agent Systems with Stealthy Context-Based Inference
item.description: arXiv:2603.11132v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Communication topology is a critical factor in the utility and safety of LLM-based multi-agent systems (LLM-MAS), making it a high-value intellectual property (IP) whose confidentiality remains insufficiently studied. Existing topology inference attempts rely on impractical assumptions, including control over the administrative agent and direct identity queries via jailbreaks, which are easily defeated by basic keyword-based defenses. As a result, prior analyses fail to capture the real-world threat of such attacks. To bridge this realism gap, we propose \textit{WebWeaver}, an attack framework that infers the complete LLM-MAS topology by compromising only a single arbitrary agent instead of the administrative agent. Unlike prior approaches, WebWeaver relies solely on agent contexts rather than agent IDs, enabling significantly stealthier inference. WebWeaver further introduces a new covert jailbreak-based mechanism and a novel fully jailbreak-free diffusion design to handle cases where jailbreaks fail. Additionally, we address a key challenge in diffusion-based inference by proposing a masking strategy that preserves known topology during diffusion, with theoretical guarantees of correctness. Extensive experiments show that WebWeaver substantially outperforms state-of-the-art (SOTA) baselines, achieving about 60\% higher inference accuracy under active defenses with negligible overhead.
item.dc:creator: Zixun Xiong, Gaoyi Wu, Lingfeng Yao, Miao Pan, Xiaojiang Du, Hao Wang

item.title: Walma: Learning to See Memory Corruption in WebAssembly
item.description: arXiv:2603.24167v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The monolithic linear memory of WebAssembly (Wasm) creates a bidirectional attack surface: a memory corruption bug in a module can compromise the host, and a compromised host can corrupt the state of a trusted module. Existing defenses either require custom runtimes or source code changes, and none can verify runtime integrity under an adversarial host. We present WALMA, the first attestation framework delivering resilience by reaction against data-centric attacks that corrupt a region of memory. We render linear memory snapshots as grayscale images and classify them with a convolutional neural network. The network reads the row-aligned structure that compiled code imposes on memory and detects corruption that byte and texture statistics miss. Our main VGG-16 detector reaches 95%--100% verdict accuracy on four of five CVE-affected applications without a single false alarm, and a 1.9M-parameter ResNet, small enough to run inside the runtime on every host call, stays within a few points of it on the same four. A Shannon-entropy analysis bounds which out-of-band edits the network can separate from valid state, and black-box evasion requires contiguous overwrites of hundreds of kilobytes to megabytes. On the 53 WABench binaries, boundary attestation costs 1.07x--1.69x, scaling with a module's exposure to the host rather than with its runtime. WALMA thus makes linear memory integrity a property a Wasm runtime can check continuously: end to end against compromised modules, and against untrusted hosts provided snapshots reach the verifier intact.
item.dc:creator: Oussama Draissi, Mark G\"unzel, Ahmad-Reza Sadeghi, Lucas Davi

item.title: AttnDiff: Attention-based Differential Fingerprinting for Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2604.05502v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Protecting the intellectual property of open-weight large language models (LLMs) requires verifying whether a suspect model is derived from a victim model despite common laundering operations such as fine-tuning (including PPO/DPO), pruning/compression, and model merging. We propose \textsc{AttnDiff}, a data-efficient white-box framework that extracts fingerprints from models via intrinsic information-routing behavior. \textsc{AttnDiff} probes minimally edited prompt pairs that induce controlled semantic conflicts, captures differential attention patterns, summarizes them with compact spectral descriptors, and compares models using CKA. Across Llama-2/3 and Qwen2.5 (3B--14B) and additional open-source families, it yields high similarity for related derivatives while separating unrelated model families (e.g., $>0.98$ vs.\ $<0.22$ with $M=60$ probes). With 5--60 multi-domain probes, it supports practical provenance verification and accountability.
item.dc:creator: Haobo Zhang, Zhenhua Xu, Junxian Li, Shangfeng Sheng, Dezhang Kong, Meng Han

item.title: Empirical Ciphertext Distinguishability Testing of KEMs and Hybrid Encryption via Deep Learning
item.description: arXiv:2604.06942v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We model indistinguishability under chosen-plaintext attack (IND-CPA) games as binary classification tasks for deep neural networks (DNNs). We apply this methodology to the public-key encryption (PKE) schemes used to construct PQC key encapsulation mechanisms (KEMs) such as ML-KEM and HQC, and to cascaded symmetric algorithms, demonstrating methodological generality. Moreover, we present a novel extension of this approach to empirical distinguishability testing of hybrid KEMs. For IND-CPA-secure schemes and their combinations, no DNN achieves accuracy significantly different from random guessing (measured via Bonferroni-corrected binomial tests), consistent with theoretical security guarantees. For insecure schemes, such as plain RSA, AES-CTR and AES-CBC with IV or counter reuse, or RC4, the DNNs classify the ciphertexts better than random guessing. Thus, this framework is shown to serve as a practical, scheme-agnostic tool for flagging distinguishable ciphertexts in both individual and composed constructions.
item.dc:creator: Simon Calderon, Niklas Johansson, Onur G\"unl\"u

item.title: BRASP: Hiding Where You Look in Encrypted Spatial Keyword Search
item.description: arXiv:2604.07797v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Searchable Encryption (SE) enables users to query outsourced encrypted data while preserving data confidentiality. However, most efficient schemes still leak the search pattern and access pattern, which may allow an honest-but-curious cloud server to infer query contents, user interests, or returned records from repeated searches and observed results. Existing pattern-hiding solutions mainly target keyword queries and do not naturally support Boolean range queries over encrypted spatial data. This paper presents BRASP, a searchable encryption scheme for Boolean range queries over encrypted spatial data. BRASP combines Hilbert-curve-based prefix encoding with encrypted prefix--ID and keyword--ID inverted indexes to support efficient spatial range filtering and conjunctive keyword matching. To hide the search pattern and access pattern under a dual-server setting, BRASP integrates index shuffling for encrypted keyword and prefix entries with ID-field redistribution across two non-colluding cloud servers. BRASP also supports dynamic updates and achieves forward security. We formalize the security of BRASP through confidentiality, shuffle indistinguishability, query unforgeability, and forward-security analyses, and we evaluate its performance experimentally on a real-world dataset. The results show that BRASP effectively protects query privacy while incurring relatively low computation and communication overhead. To facilitate reproducibility and further research, the source code of BRASP is publicly available at https://github.com/Egbert-Lannister/BRASP
item.dc:creator: Jing Zhang, Ganxuan Yang, Yifei Yang, Siqi Wen, Baiyan Li, Zhengyang Qiu, Hasan Ahmed, Muhammad Bilal

item.title: Acceptance Cards:A Four-Diagnostic Standard for Safe Fine-Tuning Defense Claims
item.description: arXiv:2605.10575v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Safe fine-tuning defenses are often endorsed on the basis of a held-out gap reduction, but the same reduction can come from sampling noise, subject artifacts, capability loss, or a mechanism that does not transfer. We introduce Acceptance Cards: an evaluation protocol, a documentation object, an executable audit package, and a claim-specific evidential standard for safe fine-tuning defense claims. The protocol checks statistical reliability, fresh semantic generalization, mechanism alignment, and cross-task transfer before treating a gap reduction as a full-card pass. Re-scored under this installed-gap protocol, SafeLoRA fails the full-card pass on Gemma-2-2B-it: under strict mechanism-class coding it fails all four diagnostics, and under a permissive shrinkage relabel it still fails three of four. This is a narrow installed-gap audit on one model family, not a global judgment of SafeLoRA's effectiveness. In a 46-cell audit, no cell satisfies the strict conjunction. The closest family is a near miss that passes reliability and mechanism checks where the required data are available, but fails the fresh-subject threshold, lacks a strict transfer pass, and carries a measurable deployment-accuracy cost.
item.dc:creator: Phongsakon Mark Konrad, Toygar Tanyel, Serkan Ayvaz

item.title: Mobius Injection: From One-Shot Prompt Injection to Sustained Resource Exhaustion in AI Agent Infrastructure
item.description: arXiv:2605.11442v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents have emerged as key intermediaries, orchestrating complex interactions between human users and a wide range of digital services and LLM infrastructures. While prior research has extensively examined the security of LLMs and agents in isolation, the systemic risk of the agent acting as a disruptive "hub" within the user-agent-service chain remains largely overlooked. In this work, we expose a novel threat paradigm by introducing Mobius Injection, a sophisticated attack that weaponizes autonomous agents into zombie nodes to launch what we define as Agent-based and -Oriented DDoS (AbO-DDoS) attacks. Mobius Injection composes known indirect prompt injection and persistent agent components through a distinct structural mechanism named Semantic Closure, which induces sustained recursive execution of agent components through a single injection event. We demonstrate that this attack is lightweight for the adversary, can evade traditional volumetric DDoS monitors and input filters calibrated for low false-positive rates, and is highly configurable, allowing for surgical targeting of specific environments or model providers. To evaluate the real-world impact, we conduct extensive experiments across three representative claw-style agents and three mainstream coding agents, integrated with 12 frontier proprietary or open-weight LLMs. Our results demonstrate that Mobius Injection achieves substantial attack success across diverse tasks, driving single-node call amplification up to 51.0x. Under coordinated multi-node pressure, each infected node still drains about 123k--127k tokens on a shared five-GPU backend; benign request latency rises by abou 23x--24x, and coordinated infections eventually saturate shared capacity until benign traffic is effectively denied service.
item.dc:creator: Zi Liang, Ronghua Li, Yanyun Wang, Qingqing Ye, Haibo Hu

item.title: Devilray: A Reconfigurable Adversarial Baseline for Revealing Blind Spots in Fake Base Station Detection
item.description: arXiv:2605.19232v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fake Base Station (FBS) detection has been a critical focus of cellular security research for over two decades. However, significant financial and regulatory barriers to accessing commercial FBS (C-FBS) devices have limited direct visibility into real-world operations, forcing detection systems to be designed and evaluated around self-built prototypes. In this paper, we present Devilray, a reconfigurable adversarial baseline to guide effective FBS detection by exploring the realistic adversarial space and identifying blind spots in detection systems -- regions of realistic adversarial behavior excluded by prevailing threat models. To this end, we establish an empirical anchor through the first academic analysis of a C-FBS, define a fundamental four-phase pipeline and seven operational feature dimensions for adversarial behaviors, and extend them with operational variants derived from 3GPP standards analysis. Through combinatorial configurations of operations from commercial practices and specifications, Devilray enables the exploration of 2,592 FBS instances, spanning diverse operational possibilities. Using Devilray, we evaluate seven currently accessible FBS detectors and uncover coverage gaps across all seven, revealing blind spots rooted in assumption-bound design and evaluation. Our work provides an empirically grounded adversarial baseline for evaluating FBS detectors and guiding future detection design, with Devilray and its configuration profiles released to vetted research groups.
item.dc:creator: Taekkyung Oh, Duckwoo Kim, Hansung Bae, Beomseok Oh, CheolJun Park, Tyler Tucker, Nathaniel Bennett, Sangwook Bae, Byeongdo Hong, Patrick Traynor, Yongdae Kim

item.title: Authenticity Debt and the Synthetic Content Threat Landscape: A Layered Framework for Trust, Provenance, and IP Governance in the Generative AI Era
item.description: arXiv:2606.00621v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has fundamentally changed how content is now produced. It has enabled how high-fidelity text, images, audio, and videos are created, modified, and redistributed at near-zero marginal cost. This shift exposes enterprises and ecosystems to a number of risks across four reinforcing authenticity layers -- authenticity, provenance, integrity, and accountability -- that traditional controls are inadequate to address in isolation. We introduce the concept of authenticity debt: the cumulative institutional liability that accumulates when organizations deploy AI-generated content without preserving verifiable origin, integrity, and accountability, deferring exposure that surfaces under regulatory, legal, or market scrutiny. This paper presents a comprehensive, multi-dimensional taxonomy of generative AI harms and attack vectors, surveys the capabilities and failure modes of technical controls including digital watermarking, provenance frameworks (C2PA, Adobe CAI), and detection technologies, and argues that no single mechanism is sufficient in open, adversarial, and evolving environments. Drawing on Zero Trust Architecture principles and enterprise governance frameworks, we propose a layered reference architecture that integrates cryptographic provenance, human-in-the-loop verification, and continuous governance to sustain defensible authenticity at scale. We further examine the regulatory landscape (EU AI Act, U.S.\ FTC, NIST AI RMF) and identify practical guiding principles for organizations seeking to build authenticity as institutional infrastructure rather than an afterthought.
item.dc:creator: Shubhashis Sengupta, Benjamin McCarty, Milind Savagaonkar, Rhine Andotra

item.title: RogueMerge: Robust and Unified Attacks against LLM Model Merging
item.description: arXiv:2606.03344v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Model merging composes specialized capabilities into a single LLM by aggregating task-specific LLMs sourced from unverified public platforms, exposing a critical supply-chain attack surface: Because any malicious behavior can be encoded into a task vector, and merging grants third-party vectors direct write access to model weights, an attacker-provided task vector can enable or amplify diverse downstream threats. Prior work only examines backdoor attacks against model merging for classifiers using static arithmetic heuristics, which fail to effectively achieve diverse attacks on generative LLMs for three reasons: (i) LLMs rely on autoregressive decoding, where even a minor parameter drift introduced by merging compounds across tokens and rapidly degrades the attack. (ii) Attackers have no knowledge of the victim's merging configurations, causing a static attack vector optimized in isolation to be easily diluted or neutralized. (iii) Practical threat induction must generalize to attack prompts unseen during optimization, which static vectors cannot adequately encode. In light of these gaps, we present RogueMerge, the first unified attack framework addressing all three challenges. To handle autoregressive generation, we replace static arithmetic with a joint optimization that explicitly enforces attack success after merging. To better simulate unknown merging settings, we formulate attack injection as a stochastic min-max optimization problem and solve it via meta-gradient descent. To generalize across heterogeneous attack prompts, we employ distributionally robust optimization and derive a tractable first-order Taylor approximation at LLM scale, with a provable error bound. Across four threats, six merging algorithms, and over 170 merged LLMs, RogueMerge consistently outperforms prior attacks. It also remains stable across diverse merging settings and resists standard defenses.

item.title: GitInject: Real-World Prompt Injection Attacks in AI-Powered CI/CD Pipelines
item.description: arXiv:2606.09935v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI agents are increasingly embedded in continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) workflows to autonomously review pull requests, triage issues, and maintain codebases. We study fully automated configurations in which external contributions invoke agents without prior human approval. Because these agents ingest untrusted content while operating with repository credentials and tools, prompt injection can have software supply chain consequences. We present GitInject, an open-source framework for evaluating prompt injection in live GitHub Actions workflows. Unlike benchmarks that simulate tool calls, GitInject provisions ephemeral repositories and executes actual workflows, exposing platform semantics such as sandbox constraints, credential handling, and permission boundaries. We use GitInject to evaluate eleven named attack scenarios across five workflows from four AI providers, covering configuration-file injection, credential exfiltration, judgment manipulation, and availability. Every provider is susceptible to at least one high-severity attack in the tested configurations. The most consequential vulnerabilities are structural: attacker-controlled configuration files from an unmerged contribution are loaded as operator-level instructions, allowing the agent--infrastructure interaction to expose credentials or corrupt review judgments. Two configuration-file attacks replicate on GitLab and Hugging Face as well as GitHub. We evaluate workflow-level countermeasures and show their coverage and utility tradeoffs. We release GitInject and all attack scenarios.

item.title: JailbreakOPT: Iterative Jailbreak Prompt Optimization with Macro-Action
item.description: arXiv:2606.11425v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Jailbreak attacks expose persistent safety weaknesses in large language models (LLMs), but existing stateless single-turn methods face a trade-off: hand-crafted prompts are expressive but static, while iterative prompt optimization can adapt but often relies on low-level mutations that require many target-model responses. We propose JailbreakOPT, a method that maintains a library of reusable prompt transformations (actions) and composes them into macro-actions for within-episode search, generating standalone attack prompts. To reuse experience across episodes, JailbreakOPT learns an action-selection policy using contextual Thompson sampling and outcomes from prior search paths. Experiments across multiple LLMs and benchmarks show that JailbreakOPT improves attack success rate (ASR) over single-action and iterative baselines. More broadly, exploration and exploitation over human-designed attack strategies can help probe residual vulnerabilities and identify failure patterns that may inform defenses aimed at broader classes of attacks.
item.dc:creator: Ge Shi, Jun Yin, Donglin Xie, Fangyi Liu, Yucan Li, Menglin Liu

item.title: General Linear-Layer Algorithms for Privacy-Preserving Transformer Inference
item.description: arXiv:2606.25349v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Two-party privacy-preserving Transformer inference today mainly follows one of two paradigms: non-interactive computation over fully homomorphic encryption (FHE), or a hybrid of FHE and secure multi-party computation (MPC). Either way, linear layers account for a large share of the compute and communication budget. Most existing systems attack this cost by designing bespoke plaintext encodings and ciphertext matrix algorithms that minimize the expensive key-switching operations. The price is tight coupling: each scheme only works with its own packing/encoding strategy, and moving data between linear and nonlinear layers still triggers online ciphertext transmission and ring-field conversion. We take a different route. Instead of optimizing within a chosen encoding, we design a series of general algorithms for linear layers that can be readily integrated into existing inference systems, based on FHE and additive secret sharing. Our algorithms work with any compatible RLWE-based scheme and plug into both non-interactive FHE and hybrid FHE-MPC pipelines. Output interfaces in proposed algorithms allow them to be composed with different downstream nonlinear layers. Relative to existing linear layer schemes, our construction removes online key switching, ciphertext transmission, and online ring-field conversion. As a complement, we further propose a fused RNS-CKKS technique that reduces the computational cost of multiplication followed by rotation. We prove correctness and semi-honest security of the proposed algorithms and quantify the resulting savings analytically.
item.dc:creator: Wenshao Yang, Zhenhua Liu, Dongdong Yao

item.title: Temporary Authority, Permanent Effects: Commit-Time Authorization for LLM Agents
item.description: arXiv:2607.10487v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: An LLM agent often acts on an approval it observed earlier: it reads the approval, prepares the request, and commits later. If the approval was withdrawn, or covers a different effect, the service can apply the change and report success. Seventeen fixed advisories from three deployed agent products document failures: an approval did not cover the executed effect, with no intervening change (12), or survived a change in the facts it depended on (5). We propose commit-time authorization (CTA), requiring at least one complete, current justification for the exact effect at commit: a live grant, current premises, ready dependencies, an exact-effect binding, and an eligible path. CommitGate selects one complete justification. The sink validates it or consumes an expiring, single-use derived grant atomically with the effect. In a five-model service study whose prompt states the authorization rule, timely notice prevented nearly all unauthorized effects for GPT, Fable, and Sonnet, and fewer for Qwen and Gemma. Without a signal, all five mostly completed tasks with unauthorized effects, even when a read could reveal the change; Fable's counts use its provider's answered requests. Protected sinks enforced the declared policy in LangChain approval flows, OpenHands coding tasks, services under cloud contention, and a transaction-runtime integration. The services and runtime refused effects that lost authority after a positive check and preserved fresh alternatives. After refusal, GPT, Fable, and Sonnet on OpenHands mostly published to a separately authorized target. Machine-checked proofs show whole-candidate selection, trace safety for mediated atomic sinks, and exact single-use transfer. With honest issuers, unique candidate IDs, and a premise required by policy, every candidate CTA accepts in the model carries a live grant given at the current version; slot-by-slot checks do not ensure this.
item.dc:creator: Igor Santos-Grueiro

item.title: AgentSnare: Learning to Delay, Divert, and Defuse Autonomous Web Penetration Agents
item.description: arXiv:2607.26998v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language model agents automate web penetration testing through observation-action loops, enabling defenders to influence decisions with deceptive decoy observations. Advanced agents can recognize and bypass static decoys, then refocus on real targets. We propose AgentSnare, a trajectory-adaptive deception system that expands a decoy environment alongside exploration. For online deployment, ShadowOS combines an LLM-driven decoy constructor with a virtual kernel. Conditioned on exploration, it generates decoy artifacts that the kernel materializes and handles consistently across interactions, sustaining long-horizon exploration. Because deploying a powerful LLM for decoy construction is costly and slow, we train a small LLM using an offline adversarial interaction-simulation framework. It synthesizes multi-round trajectories by generating candidates and retaining those that sustain simulated interactions. Across 15 CVE-Bench web applications and four attacker models, AgentSnare absorbs 49.9% of tool calls to delay attacks, retains 57.2% of post-entry actions in the decoy to divert trajectories, and grounds 89.5% of completion reports in decoy evidence to defuse threats; across 60 attacker-CVE pairs, no real target is exploited at pass@3.
item.dc:creator: Ruoyu Wang, Heng Zhao, Renjie Wu, Tianhang Zheng, Mengnan Zhao, Wanyu Lin, Kui Ren

item.title: Cost-Aware Hierarchical Multi-Agent Ransomware Detection and Family Attribution
item.description: arXiv:2609.04820v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sandbox execution and memory forensics are among the most resources intensive stages of malware triage. Static analysis can scale to millions of files while dynamic and memory analysis require minutes per sample. Because multimodal ransomware detectors often apply every modality to every sample, costs and latency rise even when static evidence suffice.We proposea cost aware Hierarchical Multi Agent System (HMAS) that frames evidence acquisition as a budgeted sequential decision problem enabling timely ransomware detection. Specialist agents generate schema validated risk signals for each modality while domain controllers aggregate evidence and coordinate analysis. The orchestrator starts with static evidence and escalates only if confidence is low or signals disagree. A locally hosted language model provides a limited, accoutable review without replacing the deterministic pipeline. Experiments on 16 ransomware families show 94.12% binary accuracy (F1 0.9376, ROC-AUC 0.9989). For multi class family attribution, it achieves 98.90% accuracy (macro-F1 0.9748). The system resolves 57.95% of the samples using static analysis alone whhile only 6.21% require the full pipeline. Compared with exhaustive cost of 12.0 units,the proposed system reduces te average cost to 6.724 units, representing approximately 44% saving. Zero day experiments further examine generalization to unseen ransomware families. Additional evaluations examine cost sensitivity and component level contribution. LLM-assisted review provides only marginal improvement in F1 while introducing additional computational overhead. Overall, the results show the potential of adaptive hierarchical multi agent orchestration to balance ransomware detection performance, family attribution analysis cost and decision latency.
item.dc:creator: Mubashar Iqbal, Hifsa Asif, Saddam Hussain Khan, Umme Zahoora, Asifullah Khan

item.title: Revisiting Certified Defense with Differential Privacy on Vision Transformers
item.description: arXiv:2609.31310v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Certified defenses that incorporate differential privacy have proven effective on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), furnishing rigorous robustness guarantees against norm-bounded adversaries. However, the certified robustness behavior of Pixel Differential Privacy (PixelDP) remains largely unexplored with the self-attention architecture now dominating the deep-learning landscape. Given that the Transformer has a profound impact on our daily applications from the digital world to the physical world, it is crucial to study certified robustness through differential-privacy-style stability. To fill this research gap, we revisit this construction in Vision Transformers and identify a failure mode that is largely hidden in the convolutional setting. When noise is injected after the patch embedding, the Laplace mechanism with the inherited grouped $\ell_1$ sensitivity bound collapses to chance-level accuracy across noise scales, whereas the Gaussian mechanism remains trainable. This contrast isolates the source of failure: not the injected noise itself, but the geometry of the sensitivity constraint. We show that the attenuation induced by the inherited $\Delta_{1,1}$ projection increases with layer width and kernel size according to a random-matrix scale $C/(\sqrt{M}+\sqrt{N})$. Replacing the $\ell_1$-type constraint with a spectral-norm constraint eliminates the collapse across datasets and architectures, but creates a fundamental obstacle: the repaired models no longer satisfy the sensitivity condition required by the standard Laplace certificate. We resolve this mismatch by deriving a dimension-free $(\varepsilon,\ \delta)$-privacy guarantee for the Laplace mechanism under $\ell_2$ sensitivity through concentration of the privacy loss.
item.dc:creator: Jun Yan, Weiquan Huang, Qixian Zhang, Yan Bai, Shutai Zhang

item.title: SkillDRE: Dual-Stage Red-Team Evolution of Agent Skills via Pre-Execution and Runtime Feedback
item.description: arXiv:2609.32400v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Agent skills package instructions, executable code, and task-specific resources into reusable artifacts that agents can improve using execution feedback. The same mechanism also enables attackers to evolve malicious skills, making them more effective and less detectable. However, a candidate skill may pass pre-execution scanning yet fail to realize its target under runtime defenses, while a revision that repairs execution may introduce new scanner findings. We introduce SkillDRE, a fully automated framework for evolving complete malicious skill packages through a dual-stage feedback loop. Given a benign task and its associated skills, SkillDRE autonomously constructs and validates a task-conditioned malicious objective and a verifiable judge rule. It then holds both fixed while evolving the skill implementation, with preservation of legitimate task capability. SkillDRE combines scanner-guided evolution with runtime-guided refinement informed by execution outcomes observed under runtime defense. Each runtime-guided revision returns to the pre-execution stage for rescanning and further optimization before re-execution, forming a cross-stage closed loop. Evaluated on SkillsBench across four victim models, SkillDRE achieves an average attack success rate of 45.28%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 40.3%, while its final submitted skills receive no SkillScan findings and largely preserve benign-task performance. These results show that two-stage defense feedback can serve as a useful learning signal for adaptive red teaming and that evaluating either defense stage in isolation can miss the resulting attack capability. Codes is available at https://github.com/whfeLingYu/SkillDRE
item.dc:creator: Pengyu Zhu, Jingyi Yang, Yi Liu, Li Sun, Sen Su

item.title: Receiver-Domain Behavioral Probing for Backdoor-Resilient Federated GPS Spoofing Detection in UAV Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.10360v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Federated learning (FL) allows unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) fleets to train a shared GPS spoofing detector without exchanging raw receiver observations. Some UAV-FL schemes use client-reported performance to determine aggregation weights, which allows compromised clients to manipulate their influence on the global model. We study an attack in which two of ten clients poison part of their data, scale their model updates, and inflate their reported accuracy. The accuracy-weighted rule produces a backdoor lift of +0.3036, compared with +0.2415 for attacked FedAvg. To address this vulnerability, we develop receiver-domain behavioral probing. The coordinator evaluates submitted models on counterfactual spoofed samples constructed by assigning benign values to discriminative GPS features and computes trust from the models' responses without using reported accuracy. With independent and identically distributed (IID) client data, our method reduces backdoor lift to -0.0265 and flags the compromised clients. It assumes an honest majority but does not require a configured Byzantine-tolerance parameter. When the number of attackers exceeds the tolerance configured for Multi-Krum, its lift increases from +0.0061 to +0.2837, whereas our method remains close to the honest baseline. We evaluate the approach using a public single-receiver dataset partitioned into simulated UAV clients and examine its limitations under strong client heterogeneity.
item.dc:creator: Will Jedrzejczak, Cole Walther, Dilpreet Gill, Moh Khalid Hasan

item.title: MAS-Guard: Unified Guardrails from Individual Agents to Multi-Agent LLM Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.28397v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Agentic AI extends large language models (LLMs) from generating responses to planning and executing complex workflows, substantially expanding their utility while exposing applications to unsafe actions, information leakage, and adversarial manipulation. Multi-agent systems further expand these capabilities through specialization and collaboration, but distributed authority, heterogeneous roles, and opaque or potentially compromised participants make safeguarding even more challenging. Existing defenses address important individual threats but provide fragmented coverage across local execution, system-level interactions, and enforcement mechanisms. We introduce MAS-Guard, a unified framework that closes this gap for safeguarding single- and multi-agent AI applications containing both instrumentable and opaque agents. Within instrumentable agents, the proposed local Agent Guardrail (A-Guard) layer applies task-specific experts to assess agentic events. At the system level, developer-owned Agent Charters and a Control Plane combine deterministic structural checks of routes, agent capabilities, and message formats with semantic assessments of roles and message content. These complementary layers enable enforcement through a shared set of interventions: allow, reflection, confirmation, and block. Evaluated across six benchmarks covering diverse single- and multi-agent scenarios with three agent LLMs from different providers, MAS-Guard reduces the overall attack success rate by 71.5-86.3% relative to unguarded agents, while meeting the utility reference criterion on benign tasks.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Kachuee, Phu Mon Htut, Sheng Li, Nikolaos Pappas, Miguel Ballesteros, Yassine Benajiba, Sujith Ravi, Dan Roth

item.title: Data-Void Exploits in Web-Searching LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2610.30365v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Web-searching Large Language Models (LLMs) have changed how users seek online information: instead of sifting through ranked lists of links, users read synthesized answers. This shift creates a new LLM vulnerability: a data-void exploit. Disinformers publish their narratives in search spaces where relevant and reliable content is scarce, i.e. data voids, then rely on the LLM's web-search to retrieve and then use, cite, or list those pages in its responses to data-void seeking prompts. Unlike classical search, where users see ranking cues and competing results, LLMs can obscure when an answer relies on sparse, unverified, or adversarial sources. We study this threat by varying the user's prompt tone - skeptical, excited, or neutral - and LLM choice - ChatGPT, Gemini, or Sonar Pro - as well as three attacker controls. The attacker can use one of five known strategies to construct and fill a data void with their narrative, host their content at varying levels of visibility from well-established, indexed domains to less established ones, and include generative-optimization engine features thought to boost citing by web-searching LLMs. We find that data-void exploits can succeed with only a single attacker controlled page. Across all conditions, attacker-content appears in LLM responses 31% of the time. User controls offer limited protection: while skeptical prompts slightly reduce success and slightly increase flagging or warnings in LLM responses, we find no evidence of large effects of prompt tone or model choice on success rates, although smaller effects cannot be ruled out. Overall, our results establish data voids as a practical inference-time attack surface for manipulating web-searching LLMs through strategically placed web content and highlight the urgent need for defenses against such exploits.
item.dc:creator: Michele Guerra, Wuyeh Jobe, Sanjana Nambiar, Christina P\"opper, Azza Abouzied

item.title: Benchmarking Classical and Quantum Machine Learning for Intrusion Detection Across Multiple Datasets
item.description: arXiv:2610.33119v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Intrusion detection is examined through a comparative benchmark of classical and quantum machine learning models on three datasets: NSL-KDD, UNSW-NB15, and MQTTEEB-D2025. The analysis focuses on how preprocessing decisions, feature selection strategies, and quantum encoding schemes shape model performance on data with differing levels of noise and complexity. A single unified pipeline is applied, covering normalization, class-imbalance handling, dimensionality reduction, and two feature selection methods: Random Forest importance and a quantum-aware approach that combines Quantum Kernel Alignment with Mutual Information (QKA-MI). Four classifiers are compared: Support Vector Machine, Random Forest, Quantum Support Vector Machine, and Pegasos Quantum SVM. The classical models perform consistently across all three datasets, whereas the quantum models depend more strongly on feature representation and kernel alignment. Quantum-aware feature selection yields marked gains for the quantum models, especially on cleaner datasets, while heterogeneous traffic remains difficult. Pegasos Quantum SVM offers a good trade-off between accuracy and computational cost, underscoring the role of preprocessing alignment in practical quantum intrusion detection.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: 2026 6th International Conference on Electrical, Computer and Energy Technologies (ICECET)
item.dc:creator: Taha M. Mahmoud, Naima Kaabouch

item.title: Provably Secure Diffusion Watermarking Against Removal Adversaries with Batched Detector Access
item.description: arXiv:2610.39189v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent latent-based watermarking methods can embed undetectable watermarks into AI-generated content. However, these approaches are vulnerable to removal attacks as their watermark detection boundaries are exposed, prompting the use of secret long-term transformations to hide these boundaries. We show that such defenses are insecure under a stronger threat model motivated by publicly reachable detectors: an adversary with batched detector access can reconstruct the transformations, permanently re-exposing the decision boundary. To address this, we propose a watermarking scheme based on a hybrid of long-term and one-time secret transformations, which prevents the reuse of structure across samples and keeps the long-term secret hidden. Besides undetectability, we show that this scheme is provably secure against removal adversaries with batched detector access, in the sense that no probabilistic polynomial-time adversary can achieve a non-negligible advantage over an adversary restricted to adding isotropic white-noise with a $\sqrt{2}\times$ larger perturbation budget, and we show this $\sqrt{2}$ factor to be tight. Evaluations on Stable Diffusion 2.1 and XL demonstrate the attack against the existing defense, and show that our scheme preserves generation quality and withstands common perturbations and targeted removal attacks.
item.dc:creator: De Zhang Lee, Ee-Chien Chang

item.title: Systematic Evaluation of Adversarial Jailbreaking Attacks and Defenses Across Seven Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.39509v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deployed in safety-critical settings must resist adversarial inputs designed to elicit harmful outputs. We present a systematic empirical evaluation of five adversarial jailbreaking attack families---direct requests, roleplay-based jailbreaking, hypothetical framing, instruction override, and obfuscation---across seven open-weight LLMs served locally: Llama-3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.2-3B, Mistral-7B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma2-9B, and Phi-4-14B. We further evaluate four defense mechanisms---keyword blacklisting, self-reminder prompting, paraphrase-based sanitization, and perplexity-based filtering---against two high-ASR models (Mistral-7B and Llama-3.1-8B) on a 20-prompt subset. Across 250 prompts per model, obfuscation attacks had the highest mean attack success rate (ASR) of any family (61.4\%), were the highest or tied-highest family for every model, and achieved nonzero success on all seven. We find that model size does not significantly predict adversarial robustness (Spearman =-0.63, p=0.13, n=7), and that the two Llama-3 generations differ markedly (16.8\% and 40.8\% ASR). Self-reminder prompting gave the largest reduction, cutting ASR from 50\% to 10\% on Mistral-7B and from 45\% to 5\% on Llama-3.1-8B (40 percentage points on each model, against matched no-defense runs). Our code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/Mdniloykhan/jailbreak-eval-7llms.
item.dc:creator: Md. Robiul Islam Niloy, Abu Sayed Md. Mostafizur Rahaman

item.title: Affine and cyclic affine equivalence of rotation-symmetric S-boxes
item.description: arXiv:2203.00778v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A rotation-symmetric S-box on $n$ bits is a vectorial Boolean function that commutes with the right cyclic shift and is therefore determined by a single Boolean function. The map $\chi$ used in Keccak is a well-known example. Ordinary affine equivalence allows arbitrary invertible affine transformations, which need not preserve rotation symmetry. We introduce \emph{cyclic affine equivalence}, in which the implementing transformations each have an invertible $k$-circulant linear part with $\gcd(k,n)=1$ and a translation vector fixed by the shift. For $n\ge3$, the two relations give the same classes of rotation-symmetric permutations exactly when $n$ is an odd prime for which $2$ is a primitive root. In every other dimension $n\ge3$, explicit constructions exhibit affine classes containing several cyclic affine classes. We derive exact class-size formulas, count cyclic affine classes for $3\le n\le9$, and classify a four-bit family of $\chi$-siblings under both relations. Finally, we characterize when a permutation is affinely equivalent to a rotation-symmetric one and apply the criterion to the Ascon S-box.
item.dc:creator: Tron Omland, Pantelimon Stanica

item.title: New classes of reversible cellular automata
item.description: arXiv:2411.00721v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Cellular automata find applications in cryptography, error correction, theoretical computer science, and the simulation of physical and biological processes. We say that a Boolean function is a proper lifting if its induced cellular automaton is reversible. This paper introduces new classes of proper liftings, constructed through compositions of landscape functions, and explores their cryptographic potential by computing indicators relevant to differential and linear cryptanalysis. We combine theoretical and computational methods to obtain a complete classification of proper liftings for diameters up to $6$. Several open problems and conjectures are posed along the way.
item.dc:creator: Jan Kristian Haugland, Tron Omland

item.title: Private Minimum Hellinger Distance Estimation via Hellinger Distance Differential Privacy
item.description: arXiv:2501.14974v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Objective functions based on Hellinger distance yield robust and efficient estimators of model parameters. Motivated by privacy and regulatory requirements encountered in contemporary applications, we derive in this paper \emph{private minimum Hellinger distance estimators}. The estimators satisfy a new privacy constraint, namely, Hellinger differential privacy, while retaining the robustness and efficiency properties. We demonstrate that Hellinger differential privacy shares several features of standard differential privacy while allowing for sharper inference. Additionally, for computational purposes, we also develop Hellinger differentially private gradient descent and Newton-Raphson algorithms. We illustrate the behavior of our estimators in finite samples using numerical experiments and verify that they retain robustness properties under gross-error contamination.
item.dc:creator: Fengnan Deng, Anand N. Vidyashankar

item.title: The Alignment Illusion: How BadReward Corrupts Text-to-Image Generation
item.description: arXiv:2506.03234v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern text-to-image generative models increasingly rely on Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) to align generated content with human preferences and safety standards. This post-training stage is critical for optimizing models toward high-fidelity and value-aligned behaviors using human preference data. However, while previous works have extensively investigated poisoning attacks against the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) stage of text-to-image training, the security vulnerabilities introduced by the RLHF process remain unexplored. In this paper, we present the first exploration into the feasibility of poisoning the RLHF process as a novel attack surface for compromising text-to-image models. We introduce BadReward, an indirect clean-label poisoning attack that manipulates reward signals to embed malicious behaviors. Our approach leverages a feature collision mechanism to produce poison preference image pairs that are visually benign, but aligned with a malicious target concept in the reward feature space. Our experiments demonstrate that this manipulation effectively corrupts the reward signal. Online RLHF further amplifies this corruption through its reward-model feedback loop, whereas offline preference optimization learns directly from the poisoned preferences. Finally, we demonstrate the real-world effectiveness of BadReward on modern text-to-image architectures, showing high attack success rates and visual stealthiness across different RLHF algorithms. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZJUICSR/BadReward.

item.title: A Survey on Agentic Security: Applications, Threats and Defenses
item.description: arXiv:2510.06445v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this work we present the first holistic survey of the agentic security landscape, structuring the field around the fundamental pillars of Applications, Threats and Defenses. We provide a comprehensive taxonomy of 274 papers that covers red-teaming, blue-teaming and domain-specific applications, attack surfaces on agentic systems, defense techniques, and both offensive and defensive evaluation frameworks. For each pillar, we first discuss the literature around the taxonomy and then perform a quantitative analysis to understand the patterns across these works. For the applications, we show their security-lifecycle coverage map, compare between red-teaming and blue-teaming agents, and analyze the adversarial use of red-teaming applications. On the threat side, we analyze the entry points and agent-loop stages that attacks target, their specificity to the agentic setting, and the threat models they assume. On the defense side, we analyze the prevailing defense strategies, their cost and security trade-offs, and where in the agent lifecycle they are deployed. Finally, we provide a deatiled cross-cutting analysis, where we map which defenses cover which attack classes and chart trends in agent architecture, backbone model usage, and data modality coverage. Taken together, these findings give a researcher a structural understanding of how agentic capabilities, vulnerabilities, and countermeasures relate to one another, and to identify where the field is concentrated and where it is thin.

item.title: PentestEval: Benchmarking LLM-based Penetration Testing with Modular and Stage-Level Design
item.description: arXiv:2512.14233v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Penetration testing is essential for assessing and strengthening system security against real-world threats, yet traditional workflows remain highly manual, expertise-intensive, and difficult to scale. Although recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) offer promising opportunities for automation, existing applications rely on simplistic prompting without task decomposition or domain adaptation, resulting in unreliable black-box behavior and limited insight into model capabilities across penetration testing stages. To address this gap, we introduce PentestEval, the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating LLMs across six decomposed penetration testing stages: Information Collection, Weakness Gathering and Filtering, Attack Decision-Making, Exploit Generation and Revision. PentestEval integrates expert-annotated ground truth with a fully automated evaluation pipeline across 346 tasks covering all stages in 12 realistic vulnerable scenarios. Our stage-level evaluation of 9 widely used LLMs reveals generally weak performance and distinct limitations across the stages of penetration-testing workflow. End-to-end pipelines reach only 31% success rate, and existing LLM-powered systems such as PentestGPT, PentestAgent, and VulnBot exhibit similar limitations, with the evaluated autonomous agents showing particularly low success rates under our benchmark settings. These findings highlight that reliable autonomous penetration testing requires stronger structured reasoning and fine-grained stage-level diagnosis. PentestEval provides the foundational benchmark needed for future research on fine-grained, stage-level evaluation, paving the way toward more reliable LLM-based automation.
item.dc:creator: Ruozhao Yang, Mingfei Cheng, Gelei Deng, Tianwei Zhang, Junjie Wang, Xiaofei Xie

item.title: Monitoring the Internal Monologue: Probe Trajectories Reveal Reasoning Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2605.18549v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) introduce new opportunities for safety monitoring through their Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning. However, CoT is not always faithful to the model's final output, undermining its reliability as a monitoring tool. To address this, we investigate the hidden representations of LRMs to determine whether future behavior can be predicted from prompt and CoT representations. By evaluating a probe at each generated token, we construct a probe trajectory, the continuous evolution of a concept's probability across the reasoning process. To characterize these temporal dynamics, we extract signal-processing features that capture volatility, trend, and steady-state behavior. We find that trajectory features help precisely where the static probe is weakest, adding 21.7 AUROC points on average, and improving in every such case where that probe falls below 70. We also present two methodological insights. First, template-based training data achieves near-parity with dynamically generated model responses, eliminating the need for a costly initial inference and labeling. Second, the use of a pooling operation is necessary: last-token methods achieve poor performance, whereas average and max pooling achieve 78.5% to 97.4% AUROC and yield stable probe trajectories. Across seven reasoning models from three families and six evaluation datasets, we find probe trajectories to be a promising signal for monitoring model behavior. Warning: This article contains potentially harmful content.

item.title: It Takes Two: Complementary Self-Distillation for Contextual Integrity in LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2605.20258v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Contextual Integrity (CI) defines privacy not merely as keeping information hidden, but as governing information flows according to the norms of a given context. As large language models are increasingly deployed as personal agents handling sensitive workflows, adhering to CI becomes critical. However, even frontier models remain unreliable in making disclosure decisions, and existing mitigation strategies often degrade underlying task performance. To overcome this privacy-utility trade-off, we propose SELFCI, a complementary self-distillation framework that decouples information suppression from task resolution. SELFCI jointly optimizes two independent reverse KL divergences over distinct teacher distributions derived from feedback: one encourages preserving task-relevant information for utility, while the other enforces minimal and appropriate disclosure. This complementary formulation induces a Product-of-Experts (PoE) target, aligning the policy with the intersection of capability and privacy requirements. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that SELFCI, without relying on costly external supervision, consistently outperforms competitive baselines such as online reinforcement learning algorithms (e.g., GRPO). These trends further extend to out-of-domain settings involving agentic workflows and accumulated private context, suggesting that SELFCI provides a practical path toward CI alignment.

item.title: Discrepancy for Random Linear Codes
item.description: arXiv:2606.24471v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We show that random linear codes (RLCs) possess nearly optimal discrepancy-type properties in a broad range of settings. Our main results are two general discrepancy theorems: one controls all translates of a fixed test, and the other controls large families of Fourier-pseudorandom tests. Two motivating examples follow: First, RLCs behave essentially like unstructured random codes for list-decoding from errors above capacity. More precisely, an RLC $C\subseteq \mathbb{F}_q^n$ of rate $1 - \frac{1}{n}\log_q|B_\rho| + \varepsilon$, where $|B_\rho|$ is the volume of a radius-$\rho$ Hamming ball in $\mathbb{F}_q^n$, satisfies $|C \cap B| = (1\pm o(1)) \frac{|C|\cdot |B|}{q^n}$ simultaneously for all radius-$\rho$ Hamming balls $B$ with high probability. This significantly strengthens the best prior results, which follow from work by Blinovsky (1987, 1990) and Levitin (1988) on the covering properties of RLCs. Second, over prime fields, RLCs behave essentially like unstructured random codes for zero-error list-recovery, and list-recovery from erasures, above capacity. More precisely, for a prime $q>2$ and input list size $2\leq \ell\leq q-1$, an RLC $C\subseteq \mathbb{F}_q^n$ of rate $1-\log_q \ell+\varepsilon$ will satisfy $|C \cap S| = (1\pm o(1)) \frac{|C|\cdot \ell^n}{q^n}$ simultaneously for all combinatorial rectangles $S=S_1\times S_2\times\cdots\times S_n$, where $|S_i|=\ell$ for all $i$, with high probability. An analogous result also holds when we can bound $|S_i|$ only for some of the $i$'s. We use this to show the abundance of locally leakage-resilient $n$-party linear ramp secret sharing schemes with any linear reconstruction threshold and sublinear threshold gap $O(n/\log n)$ over fields of polynomial size $q=\Theta(n^\gamma)$ for a constant $\gamma\in(0,1/5)$. Prior work was stuck at reconstruction thresholds above $n/2$ for both threshold and ramp schemes.

item.title: Removing Speech, Keeping Activities: Speech Removal for Privacy-Preserving Acoustic Sensing in Assisted Living
item.description: arXiv:2609.02376v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Acoustic sensing can monitor the daily activities of older adults without cameras or wearables, yet the possibility of capturing private conversations remains a barrier to its deployment. The engineering application addressed in this paper is privacy-preserving acoustic monitoring of daily activities in assisted living. Our contribution in artificial intelligence is a speech-removal front end: a U-Net that masks the short-time Fourier transform of ambient audio and returns a waveform in which speech is suppressed and the sounds needed for activity recognition are kept. The model is trained only on synthetic mixtures of public sounds and speech, so no speech has to be recorded in the target homes. We evaluate it with group-disjoint cross-validation on environmental and domestic sound datasets mixed with reverberant speech, on speech from unseen corpora and on real home recordings, and measure privacy with three voice activity detectors, Whisper speech recognition and a speaker-verification attack. With speech 5 dB above the background, the macro-averaged F1 score of activity recognition is 0.574 and 0.661 after removal on the two datasets, compared with 0.233 and 0.178 without processing, and higher than that of speech enhancement, speech separation and detector-gated muting at every speech level. Whisper recovers 5.2% of the spoken words, compared with 89.0% without processing and a chance floor of 2.2%. On the real recordings, the speech proportion estimated by a voice activity detector falls from 8.5% to 2.7%. The method reduces, but does not eliminate, spoken content and speaker identity.
