item.title: Proximity Gaps for Gabidulin Codes and Applications
item.description: arXiv:2609.09838v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Proximity gaps are central to the soundness of interactive oracle proofs of proximity (IOPPs) and polynomial commitment schemes (PCSs). An $[n,k,d]$ linear code $C\subseteq\mathbb F^n$ has a $\delta$-proximity gap with error $\epsilon$ if, for every $u_0,u_1\in\mathbb F^n$, either all points on $\ell_{u_0,u_1}=\{u_0+\alpha u_1:\alpha\in\mathbb F\}$ are $\delta$-close to $C$, or at most an $\epsilon$ fraction are. Although proximity gaps for Hamming-metric codes are well understood, their rank-metric counterparts remain largely unexplored despite their applications in coding theory and cryptography. In this work, we study proximity gaps for linear rank-metric codes and their cryptographic applications. First, we show that every $[n,k,d]$ linear rank-metric code $C$ over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$ admits a proximity gap for every $\delta\le(d-1)/(3n)$, with error at most $q^{e+1}/q^m$, where $e=\lfloor\delta n\rfloor$. For Gabidulin codes, we improve the gap to $(d-1)/(2n)$ with error $10q^{n-1}/q^m$. These two proximity gaps match those for general linear Hamming-metric codes and Reed--Solomon (RS) codes, respectively. We prove the $(d-1)/(2n)$ bound is tight by constructing an infinite family of constant-rate Gabidulin codes and affine lines $\ell_{u_0,u_1}$ on which a $1-o(1)$ fraction of points are $d/(2n)$-close to the code, while $u_1$ is at least $3d/(4n)$-far from it. At $\delta=(d-1)/(2n)$, a further counterexample gives a lower bound of order $q^{n-1}/q^m$ on $\varepsilon$, matching our upper bound up to a constant factor. As applications, we construct an IOPP for interleaved Gabidulin codes by adapting the Ligero IOPP for interleaved RS codes. We then adapt the Ligero-based PCS for ordinary polynomials to obtain a $q$-linearized polynomial commitment scheme. To our knowledge, this is the first PCS framework based on rank-metric error-correcting codes.
item.dc:creator: Songsong Li, Chaoping Xing, Chen Yuan, Ruiqi Zhu

item.title: Who Audits Whom, on What Substrate, with What Evidence? An Independence-Graded Audit Protocol for Agentic AI
item.description: arXiv:2609.18272v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Agentic AI systems plan, invoke tools, and act with limited supervision; they are now both the subject of audits and, increasingly, the auditor. Independence-the foundation of assurance-is still applied to them as a binary. We argue that it must be graded along three orthogonal axes: principal independence (who controls the auditor), substrate independence (an auditor that shares the auditee's foundation-model family, toolchain, or guardrails fails with the auditee), and evidence independence (whether evidence is attestable rather than self-reported). Each axis has precedent; the contribution is to grade all three on a single audit, aggregate them by the weakest link, and apply the same rubric when the auditor is itself an agent. We give the model a formal basis by transplanting the beta-factor model of common-cause failure from reliability engineering. We also provide a seven-step protocol whose outputs a third party can verify, a structural detectability analysis of a procurement-controls agent audited at three grades, and a closed-form study of the model in which, at a declared common-mode share of 0.90 for a same-family auditor and a declared reporting probability of 0.6 for an internal team, a conventional internal audit of an agent-a real audit team, a second agent, and provider logs-surfaces 5.9% of the faults it could in principle see and, independently of those two values, none at all in half of the fault classes. Because an evidence grade says who could have altered a record, not what the record covers, every load-bearing record also carries a declared-scope predicate, and reports carry a false-flag rate beside the detection floor wherever the auditor's own performance has been measured. We map the triple to the EU AI Act as amended, ISO-IEC 42006, UK public-sector risk-management guidance, and audit-regulator practice.
item.dc:creator: Mohamed Chahine Ghanem, Baidaa Al-Bander

item.title: Temporal Liquidity Crossing for Blockchains: An EIP-1559 Extension for Admission Below the Base Fee
item.description: arXiv:2610.30595v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Transactions differ in how their value changes with execution time and relative position. Ethereum's EIP-1559 lets them compete through fee fields, but a fee bid gives no enforceable claim to an earlier position in the block, and no way to express willingness to accept a later one. Its base fee is a hard admission floor. We introduce temporal liquidity markets (TLM), a framework for crossing complementary temporal requirements: transactions seeking early-region execution (consumers) can fund transactions that opt into exclusion from that region (providers). Selected consumers complete within the early region and are ordered among themselves by authorization density, both validator-checked. In our block-local EIP-1559 extension, providers may be admitted below the base-fee floor. Under TLM regulation, funding-conditioned and capacity-capped provider gas is excluded from the ordinary EIP-1559 controller input. Counting it there instead raises the base fee and displaces ordinary demand at a positive base-fee fixed point. Exclusion lets the controller regulate ordinary demand at its original target and preserves the no-TLM ordinary allocation by construction; in synthetic experiments it raises total utilization with funded gas. Selected consumers pay their signed authorizations, which fund provider shortfalls; the surplus is burned. We state an adversary model with strategic senders and builders and prove eight properties under it, among them validator-checked rule validity, full burn of the base fee, and no subsidy. An inserted consumer bid cannot raise any other consumer's charge. With a provider fee-cap floor, a small, capped inclusion fee and a consumer allowance tied to funded provider gas by a large enough link ratio, no finite set of consumer bids or providers that the builder inserts raises its direct fee payoff.

item.title: Cheap Reverse Engineering and What It Will Do
item.description: arXiv:2610.35633v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generative AI is putting the law of reverse engineering (RE) under severe strain. Existing IP and technology laws assume that RE is expensive and time-consuming, and that it requires specialized expertise. They generally allow it, but they rely on its difficulty as a filter to separate (permissible) RE from (impermissible) copying and theft. Generative AI is changing this equation by making \RE much faster, cheaper, and easier. AI systems can identify hardware components, extract firmware, decompile object code, and clone entire apps. The resulting struggle between technology vendors and reverse engineers will challenge a wide range of laws, including trade secret, copyright, anti-circumvention, computer misuse, and contract. In this article, we describe the ways in which AI is changing \RE, map these new practices onto existing laws, and sketch ways that the legal system could respond and their associated trade-offs.
item.dc:creator: Ilan Mandel, Madiha Zahrah Choksi, Joey Castillo, Sebastian Benthall, James Grimmelmann

item.title: Efficient Scalable Oversight via Rewinding
item.description: arXiv:2610.40535v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Scalable oversight asks how a weak verifier can check the outputs of computations performed by more powerful AI systems. One proposed approach uses relativizing interactive proofs, in which a weak verifier checks the output of a complex oracle-aided computation by interacting with one or more powerful provers. A prominent example is debate, which is highly efficient but assumes that one of two powerful AI models, or provers, is truthful. For certain classes of oracle-aided computations, this assumption can be removed, but at substantially greater computational cost. In this work, we introduce \emph{rewindable interactive proofs} (RIPs), a new model of relativizing interactive proofs for scalable oversight. In an RIP, the verifier may rewind the prover to an earlier state of the interaction and continue from there. This is possible when the prover is an AI model, since the verifier can save a snapshot of the model's state and later restore it. We construct a relativizing RIP for computations whose outputs are robust to changing a small fraction of oracle answers. Our construction is more efficient than prior relativizing proofs that do not assume a truthful prover, and it uses no cryptography. In our construction the honest prover runs in time linear in that of the original computation, and the verifier, after a one-time preprocessing step, runs in time nearly linear in the input length (which can be much smaller than the computation itself). We implement our protocol, report a preliminary MNIST experiment, and show that an RIP can be faster than a state-of-the-art deployed proof system. RIPs may be of independent interest. Rewinding is possible whenever the verifier controls the prover's machine, for example when the prover runs on trusted hardware or in a virtual machine whose state can be checkpointed.
item.dc:creator: Ziyi Guan, Yael Tauman Kalai, Ron Rothblum, Zoe Xi
